Dimitrios Kyriakos designed the four on the avenue, Kimon Laskaris the four behind. They are often called among the first apartment buildings in Greece, Central European functionalism in reinforced concrete with wide courtyards between the slabs.

For decades the state wanted them gone; the Council of State blocked demolition in 2003 and 2009 and the surviving blocks were listed. Many flats are empty or occupied by a residents' collective, others still house descendants of the first families. Bullet marks from December 1944 survive on some walls.
In early 2026 the Attica Region tendered €15 million to restore four blocks as social housing by 2028. Walk the courtyards in daylight and be discreet with the camera: people live here.
prosfygika.s: Athens master research (Oct 2026); Council of State rulings 2003, 2009. Map pin approximate.

p: The blue modernist block over Exarchia Square was designed by Kyriakos Panayotakos in 1932–33, with a colour scheme by the painter Papaloukas. Le Corbusier, visiting for the 1933 CIAM congress that produced the Athens Charter, is reported to have said 'C'est très beau'.
Its ground floor held the café Floral, a left-wing meeting place, until 2016. Today it is one of the best-known images of interwar Athens.

Kypseli was the modern suburb of the 1930s, and Fokionos Negri its showpiece: a long planted boulevard lined with the first modernist apartment blocks. The Lanara block (1938, engineer I. Zolotas) is the best of them, purist with Art Deco touches; its basement served as a shelter in the Occupation.

It was threatened with demolition and listed in 2006. Walk the street from no. 7 (1932, the first modern block here) and no. 9 (Protopapa, 1933) up to here, then turn into Eptanisou for the Bonis shelter block.
lanara.s: Archive of Modern Monuments (eie.gr); Atenistas Kypseli guide; catisart.gr.

protopapa.t: Protopapa block and the first Fokionos Negri blocks
p: No. 7 (N. Papadakis, 1932) and no. 9 (Protopapa, 1933) are the first modern blocks on Fokionos Negri, the start of the 1930s modernist street. Imvrou 22, nearby, is well kept apart from a clumsy added top floor.

Leonidas Bonis designed this block in 1938 for the shipowner Voulgaris, and drew an anti-aircraft shelter into the original plans. It is still there: a central room for 63 people with toilets, a kitchen and working hand-cranked steel doors, documented by urban speleologists in 2014.
Between 1936 and 1940 about 400 public shelters were built in Attica; private ones like this are rarer and better preserved. The shelter is not open; the building is the stop.

Dourgouti was a refugee settlement: the 'Italika' row houses of 1924 and a group of seven interwar blocks survive and now house newer migrants. During the Occupation blockade of 1944 the Armenian quarter here was burned.
dourgouti.s: Myofa PhD thesis; omadaasty.blogspot. Map pin approximate.

p: One of the largest refugee housing estates in Athens: the two-storey houses of 1936 and then 71 apartment blocks, 2,030 flats in all. A good second stop after the Prosfygika for the scale of the 1920s–30s refugee housing effort.

After the 2004 Games the athletes' flats went to workers' housing families, but the administration, retail and sports buildings were abandoned; the admin building was caught up in the Vatopedi land-swap scandal. Graffiti on the fences reads 'Dead Zone'. An abandoned building at the entrance burned on 21 July 2026.

hellinikon.t: Hellinikon: Saarinen terminal and the new park
p: Athens's airport from 1938 to 2001 is now the largest building site in Greece. What is kept tells the old story: Eero Saarinen's East Terminal (designed 1960–69), the control tower, listed hangars, a stretch of runway and the 2004 canoe-slalom course are all to be reused as features of the new Ellinikon park.

After the airport closed, the field lay derelict for two decades with Olympic Airways planes still parked on the apron and the 2004 Olympic venues rotting at its edge. Demolition began in 2020; the Sports Park opened in stages from July 2026, and the Saarinen terminal is meant to become an exhibition building.
The 'abandoned' layer is effectively gone. Come for the terminal's long marble-and-concrete front and the scale of the change; the Experience Centre shows the plans.
hellinikon.s: Protothema (June 2026); Ta Nea, To Vima (July 2026); Architectural Record.

p: A curved stadium of steel and concrete on the Faliro shore, built for the 2004 beach-volleyball tournament, with 9,600 seats round a sand court now turned to weeds. AFP photographed the smashed windows and dust-caked stands in February 2024; it has hosted almost nothing since the Games.

It became the picture editors' shorthand for the cost of 2004. The Attica Region's Aenaon Park plan for the whole Faliro bay would turn the bowl into an open-air amphitheatre; the neighbouring Tae Kwon Do hall was conceded to the Region in January 2026.
Don't climb the fences. The best view is from the coastal promenade and the footbridge.
faliro-volley.s: AFP (Feb 2024); Attica Region Aenaon Park presentation; newmoney.gr (2026). Map pin approximate.

p: Built for Olympic badminton in 2004 and later run as a large theatre, the Goudi hall had a fire on 12 July 2026. What state it is in now was not checked; treat as a lead.
goudi-badminton.s: Protothema headline (Jul 2026). Map pin approximate; not verified.

p: In the pine forest above Melissia stand the concrete wings of a Bauhaus-era sanatorium, balconies turned to the sun for tuberculosis patients. A 1928 decree took about 100 stremmata for it, and it ran as the 'Penteli Sanatorium' from 1930, later as the IKA hospital until 2016. Since then it has been stripped and burned.

Penteli's dry air made it the 'Greek Davos': several sanatoria went up on its slopes between the wars. The Daou sanatorium nearby was a resistance hideout, the Bobolas wing and the Naval Sanatorium decay in the same woods.
Visitors in reviews mention vagrants and broken glass; keep to the outside. A redevelopment as a health park has been announced more than once (plans of 52 to 75 stremmata).
papadimitriou-sanatorium.s: virus.com.gr; vrilissianews.gr; adarch.gr; Athens Social Atlas.

p: Above the Rafina crossroads, a stone-built sanatorium stands roofless in the pines. Its staff were members of ELAS during the Occupation and it served as a hideout; a nurse was executed in 1944.

On the Mont Parnes road, a long ruin with empty window rows: a 1930s sanatorium, then an EOT Xenia hotel, then a tourism school that closed in 1980. The 1999 earthquake damaged it further. Urban explorers call it the most visited ruin in Greece. Pair with the 'Aeras' station and the casino.

Next to Larissa station stands the old terminus of the metre-gauge network to the Peloponnese (Athens–Corinth from 1885), which from 1929 also ran the Lavrio trains. It closed in 2005; the whole metre-gauge Peloponnese network has been suspended since 2011.
spap-station.s: Athens master research (Oct 2026). Map pin approximate.

p: Founded in 1909, the Lipasmata (fertiliser) works grew to about 250,000 m² and 109 buildings on the Drapetsona shore, one of the largest chemical plants in Europe. Most was demolished around 2003; what was kept now stands in a public park: the power station, the glass-works chimney and silo, the water tower, the chemistry institute, the Krakari conveyor gantry.

For a chemist it is a lesson in the Haber-era fertiliser industry and its cost: the plant was notorious for pollution and for its workers' strikes. The park's own site says it closed in 1993; other sources say 1999.
Walk the full seafront path from the north entrance to Krakari; ships for Piraeus pass close.
The textile giant's Megalo Pefko mill opened in 1950 as the first new factory of the postwar recovery; Time praised it in 1962. It closed in 1992 and stands empty on the road to Megara.

On the slopes of Parnitha, George I bought Tatoi in 1872 and the royal family spent summers here among farms, stables, vineyards and forest. After the monarchy was abolished in 1974 the estate decayed for decades; the 2021 Parnitha fire burned up to the royal cemetery, whose mausoleum and church survived.

A €70 million Culture Ministry project is turning the historic core into three museums; about 4,350 objects are to be shown in the palace, out of more than 100,000 recovered and conserved. Princess Irene was buried here in January 2026.
The landscape cemetery in the woods is the stop for this map. Reports in October 2026 put the opening in December.
tatoi.s: To Vima English (2026); Greek City Times (Oct 2026); Neos Kosmos (Jan 2026).

p: A bare island 2.5 nautical miles off Lavrio held political prisoners from 1946–47 to the late 1950s; up to about 100,000 passed through (a high estimate), among them Mikis Theodorakis and Yannis Ritsos. Repentant inmates were made to build copies of classical monuments. In the massacre of the First Sapper Battalion (29 Feb–1 Mar 1948), guards killed an estimated 350 prisoners.
It was declared a historic site in 1989. What remains are foundations, camp buildings and small churches on a dry ridge, and the silence.

Sotiria was Athens's great tuberculosis hospital. In 1936 Georgakopoulos and Despotopoulos (later the architect of the Athens Conservatory) designed its kitchen, laundry and dormitory building and the 'Mega Laikon' hospital wing, listed among the key modern works in Greece. Which buildings stand unaltered is still to be checked.
sotiria.s: Giamarelos (UCL, 2016) list of key works; Despotopoulos biography (Benaki). Map pin approximate; not verified.

p: The brick halls and red-and-white chimney on the Keratsini waterfront are the Agios Georgios power station, which made electricity for Athens from 1928. Locals call it the Drakos, the dragon. In October 1944 ELAS fighters held it against the retreating Germans, who meant to blow it up: the 'Battle of the Electric', remembered by an exhibition inside since 2017.
The historic plant stopped producing in 2012 (efsyn, Parliament); two later gas units stayed on reserve. In 2023 the Environment Ministry listed the historic buildings, façades and the chimney.
Pair with the Lipasmata park a short walk south and the Faliro station for the full story of Athens's electricity.
keratsini-ps.s: efsyn.gr; avgi.gr; VI.D.A. archive; ΦΕΚ 2023 listing. Map pin approximate.

p: Built in 1903 to power the electric railway and the city, the Neo Faliro station was the first large thermal plant in Greece. It ran as a reserve until 1972, was listed in 1986 and became a PPC training school in part; the historic hall stands derelict.
Art shows have used the ruined wing: composer Dimitris Kamarotos once hung an electric guitar from the roof as a giant pendulum. A 1940s pipeline linked it to Keratsini.
faliro-ps.s: lifo.gr; vida-omada; filoibenaki.gr; oneman.gr. Map pin approximate.

p: One of the 'ghost factories' of Pireos Street: CHROPEI made paints from 1899 to 1989; the listed complex passed to the Development Ministry in 2019 and stands empty. IVI and other works nearby are in the same state.
A 28,000 m² former industrial complex with ten listed concrete buildings, the Athens Festival's summer venue. The Culture Ministry plans a permanent conversion.

Athens had no reliable water until the 1920s. The Ulen contract (1924) brought the Marathon dam, inaugurated in 1929 and faced in white marble over a core of crushed-marble concrete with volcanic ash, and the 13.4 km Boyati tunnel that carried the water to Galatsi; about 450 men worked on the tunnel round the clock until 1931.
The dam is the only one in the world clad in marble. Ulen's 35 mm construction film survives. The small EYDAP museum by the crest tells the story.
marathon-dam.s: eydap.gr; el.wikipedia (Ulen); marathonpress.gr. Map pin approximate.

p: The Attica Railways line to Lavrio carried passengers until 1957 and was abolished in 1962. At Thorikos rails, a railway bridge at the fishing-shelter entrance and a decaying station remain; the small Daskaleio station has been restored, and rails resurface on Mesogeia roads (local report, Nov 2026).
lavrio-line.s: el.wikipedia; tanea.gr; lavriaki.gr (Nov 2026). Map pin approximate.

p: At Kyprianos, on the edge of Lavrio, the Compagnie Française des Mines du Laurium built its metallurgical works in 1875–76. Today 245 stremmata and 41 buildings are a listed Technological and Cultural Park run by the National Technical University (NTUA), with equipment still in place: the Mechanourgeio (machine shop, 1875–95) keeps its machinery and is being turned into a Mining–Metallurgy Museum, still 'being formed' in late 2024.

The silver that paid for the fleet at Salamis came from these hills. In the 1860s Italian (Serpieri) and French companies came to resmelt the ancient slag, then reopened the mines; their story continues at Kamariza (the Serpieri shaft), in the Souriza valley (ancient washeries) and in Lavrio port, where the 1888 iron ore-loading bridge is being restored with €9.5m from the Green Fund.
St Barbara's Catholic church stands on the slope above; her icon is set into the rock by a gallery inside the Park. There is a café and a children's play area.
lavrio-mines.s: ltcp.ntua.gr; el.wikipedia; tovima.gr; eclass-b.uoa.gr and skai.gr (museum status, 2024); Green Fund 2026 programme.

p: On a hill near Keratea lie the launch pads, bunkers and control buildings of a NIKE surface-to-air missile battery. The Greek Air Force formed 350 Squadron in 1960 with four flights: Keratea, Hymettus, Parnitha and Kithairon. It joined NATO's nuclear role in 1964; nuclear warheads were held by a small US custody detachment.
The nuclear role ended in January 1989 and the unit moved to Sedes in 2005, leaving Keratea empty. Of the four Attica sites it is the only one documented and accessible.
Drone footage shows the layout well; on the ground, look for the missile magazines and the separate radar hill.
keratea-nike.s: haf.gr via parapolitika.gr; irafina.gr; newsbeast.gr; Nike Historical Society. Map pin approximate.

p: A gatehouse with twin sentry boxes, burned-out buildings and antenna bases on one of Parnitha's summits, abandoned for over 25 years and burned in the 2007 fire. The view takes in the whole basin.

Past Agios Panteleimon on Penteli, large dishes and looted buildings mark a military telecom station that served NATO communications until about the late 1990s. It was probably part of ACE High, NATO's chain of 'troposcatter' stations that bounced radio off the lower atmosphere from Norway to Turkey.

Local stories say it relayed Scandinavian signals to the US, and a BBC piece repeated the claim that NATO took Pentelic marble for satellites: folklore, but good folklore. Whether this is one site or two with the military works near the Davelis cave is unresolved.
penteli-nato.s: irafina.gr; newsbeast.gr. Map pin approximate; not verified.

p: Just north of trig point 827 on Hymettus, next to the last OTE mast, are the foundations of a German 40th Signals Regiment post of 1942. Locals call it the German radar; local writers think the radar was a story the Germans spread.

navcommsta.t: US Naval Communications Station, Nea Makri
p: At Brexiza, the US Navy built a communications station from 1953, mostly underground. It closed in 1990 and was handed back in 2004; it is now an athletic and cultural park. How much of the underground part survives is unchecked.

Inside Ardittos hill runs the largest shelter in Attica, for about 1,300 people. Sources disagree on its origin: Skai says the Germans built it in 1943–44; others say it was a prewar air-defence coordination centre that the Germans took over as an ammunition store, used by the resistance afterwards.
Three of its four entrances have been sealed by building; the one left makes it unsafe. Its exact entrance is not public. Stand on the hill above the stadium and imagine the tunnels below.
ardittos-shelter.s: skai.gr; protothema.gr; parapolitika.gr. Map pin approximate; not verified.

p: Around 1936 a shelter was cut about 100 metres into the rock of Lycabettus, next to the cave church of Agioi Isidoroi, with two entrances. Reports describe it as bigger and in better condition than the Ardittos shelter. It is closed; visit the cave church and look for the sealed openings.
lycabettus-shelter.s: parapolitika.gr; in.gr; aftodioikisi.gr (Mar 2026). Map pin approximate.

p: Under a late-1930s modernist block, two reinforced chambers with steel-shuttered vents survive. They were used during the December 1944 fighting and opened to the public for an art show called 'Bunker'.
A basement shelter of about 80 m² in a listed building 50 metres from Parliament, reported in good condition. Closed; a pass-by stop on the way to Kolonaki.
Piraeus was bombed hard in 1941–44. On Kastella a two-storey Metaxas-era shelter stands abandoned, and a smaller one with stone walls and a concrete barrel vault lies on Profitis Ilias hill.
Along the rocky Peiraiki coast, concrete emplacements of German coastal batteries survive empty; the guns were removed in 1944.

The best preserved of Attica's coastal fortifications: three intact pillboxes, a gun base and trenches on the hill above Porto Rafti. A graffitied pillbox at Legrena (reported Aug 2026) and a neglected beach pillbox at Varkiza complete the set.
porto-rafti-pillboxes.s: skai.gr; lavriaki.gr; mixanitouxronou.gr. Map pin approximate.

p: For decades the Gulf of Elefsina was where Greece left its dead ships; AP called it 'an environmental bomb'. The state began removing hulks in 2018, so what remains in 2026 is uncertain. Combine with the sanctuary of Eleusis.
elefsina-wrecks.s: AP; Athens master research (Oct 2026). Map pin approximate.

p: Six metres under a smart office building off Panepistimiou, a 1938 gas-proof shelter of the National Insurance company became the cells of the German Kommandantur. The prisoners' graffiti has been conserved: names, dates, calendars, drawings of planes and ships, even a small Hitler portrait, scratched into doors and plaster. The outlines of the isolation cells are marked on the floor.
People were held here for anything from resistance to 'stealing bread' or climbing on a tram. From here many went on to Haidari.
Free and rarely busy. The man at the desk answers questions; little is in English, so read up before.
korai-4.s: Korai 4 Memorial Site; in.gr; Google Places (hours).

p: Next to the entrance of a Hondos Center store stands Thanasis Apartis's relief of a bound, naked man with a noose and the words 'This used to be the Gestapo hellhole 1941–1944'. The house was demolished in 1980; the iron cell door kept in the memorial is all that survives of it.
This was the SS and Gestapo interrogation centre; prisoners went on to Haidari. A historian of the Occupation told AFP in 2024 that in another European country this would be a museum.

On 1 May 1944 the Germans shot 200 communist prisoners here in batches of twenty, in reprisal for the killing of a German general. Most were long-term prisoners from Akronauplia brought from Haidari. Eyewitnesses describe them singing as they walked to the wall. A black granite memorial lists the names inside what is now a park with a café and playground.

In February 2026 twelve unseen photographs of the condemned surfaced on eBay; the Culture Ministry declared them a protected monument, and within hours vandals smashed the memorial plaques. The municipality promised to repair and upgrade the site.
Weizsäcker came here in 1987; Tsipras made it his first stop as prime minister in 2015. The National Resistance Museum is nearby.
kaisariani-range.s: Greek City Times (Feb 2026); Atlas Obscura; Athens master research (Oct 2026).

p: Over 21,000 people passed through Haidari between September 1943 and September 1944, including Jews deported to Auschwitz; a former inmate estimated some 2,000 executions. Block 15 was the solitary and condemned block, the start point for the 200 of Kaisariani. It was listed in 1987 and is decaying inside an active camp.
haidari-block15.s: Hellenic Ministry of National Defence; block15.aueb.gr; D2 (Nov 2026).

p: On 17 August 1944 German troops and Security Battalions sealed Kokkinia (Nikaia), herded the men into the square and had hooded informers pick out resistance members. Those chosen were shot in this walled factory yard, the Mantra: 72 men and 3 women. The Blockade's total dead is given as over 200 (Attica Region) to 315 (Wikipedia).

The hall keeps ricochet marks in the walls and the wooden gate, the 'Portara', listed as a monument. Inside, a portrait of almost every victim. Celtic-cross graffiti was sprayed on it in September 2024.
Visitors call it one of the most moving museums in Athens. Pair with Plateia Osias Xenis (the selection point) and the Third Cemetery, where the dead are buried.
Kantzilieris's bronze of 1980 stands where 114 men were executed in August 1944. The exact wall is not identified in the sources found.

Nea Smyrni, built for refugees from Smyrna, saw heavy fighting in December 1944. A local walk links the plaque on Plateia Skatzouraki, the ELAS hospital at Korai and Sofouli, and the 1920s Iosifogleio orphanage on Syngrou, requisitioned in 1941.

beth-shalom.t: Beth Shalom and the Holocaust memorial
p: On Friday 24 March 1944 the Germans used the regular registration at the Beth Shalom synagogue to arrest the Jews of Athens; most were deported to Auschwitz. The Community gives 23 March; the 1947 plaque says 24. Across the street is the old Romaniote synagogue.
A few minutes away, Dimitris Maganias's Holocaust memorial (2010) is a Star of David broken into pieces, each pointing to a Greek Jewish community. The Jewish Museum on Nikis tells the rest.
beth-shalom.s: tovima.gr; maxmag; Jewish Museum of Greece.

p: The Averof prison held political prisoners for eighty years, from the Metaxas years to the junta. It was demolished in 1972 and the courts built on the site; a stele in the courtyard and the name on the 813 bus are what remain.

Bouboulinas 18, once a clinic and a hotel, was the Security Police headquarters of the junta until 1971; prisoners were beaten on the soles of the feet (falanga) in a room on the roof. It was demolished shortly before the junta fell, and a block of flats stands on the site.
Next door, nos. 20–22 (the Logothetopoulos building, now a Culture Ministry office) is often wrongly pointed out as the torture building. In 1971 the Security moved to Mesogeion 14–18.

When the Security Police left Bouboulinas in 1971, they moved here, to a 1960 office block now used by the General Secretariat for Research and Innovation. Two original basement cells survive. Plaques at the entrance and in the basement have marked them since November 2017.
Historian Kallivretakis documented the building for the National Hellenic Research Foundation in 2019. Whether the cells open around 17 November was not confirmed.

In what is now Freedom Park, behind the US Embassy, four low buildings were the Special Interrogation Section of the Military Police (EAT-ESA), the junta's worst torture centre. Alexandros Panagoulis was held and beaten here after his attempt on Papadopoulos in 1968. A small anti-dictatorship memorial occupies one building.

On 13 August 1968 Alexandros Panagoulis detonated a bomb in a 7 m culvert under the coast road as the dictator Papadopoulos drove by; it missed. The junta put up a monument 'in remembrance', paid for by the 32nd Marines. Whether it still stands is unknown.
loumbarda.s: mixanitouxronou.gr; mesogianews. Map pin approximate; not verified.

p: Panagoulis survived torture and prison, became an MP and was investigating junta files when he died in a car crash on Vouliagmenis Avenue on 1 May 1976. Many still consider it suspicious. The metro station carries his name.

On 14 November 1973 students occupied the Polytechnic and broadcast against the junta from a radio in the building. In the early hours of the 17th a tank drove through the main gate. The twisted gate is preserved in the courtyard beside the memorial; a bronze head lies on the ground.
Every 17 November a march goes from here to the US Embassy, and the gate is covered in flowers. Enter from Stournari on ordinary days.

A marble plaque and an informal shrine at Tzavella and Mesologgiou mark where a special guard shot Alexandros Grigoropoulos on 6 December 2008. The killing set off the largest riots in Greece in decades.

The Army Share Fund building (listed 1994) was the seat of the German military administration during the Occupation. Today it is the City Link complex, home to Athénée (ex-Zonar's) and the Attica department store, which stands on the site of Flokas café.
Kaisariani, a refugee suburb called 'Little Moscow' for its resistance, keeps bullet-marked refugee blocks and a mural. Walk here after the Shooting Range.

guillotine-nymphs.t: Otto-era guillotine site, Hill of the Nymphs
p: The guillotine came to Greece with the Bavarians. In 'La Grèce contemporaine' (1854) Edmond About places executions near the Cave of the Nymphs below the Observatory hill. Nothing marks the spot; the last guillotine itself is in the Criminology Museum.
guillotine-nymphs.s: vradini; insider.gr; About (1854). Location not verified.

p: In the Athens Medical School at Goudi, the Criminology Museum keeps the last guillotine used in Greece (last on 11 April 1912), the preserved heads of 19th-century bandits, tattooed skin, embryos in formalin and murder weapons from old cases.
Getting in is the hard part: Google reviews in 2026 say the phone goes unanswered and requests are refused. Worth one call.

From 1889 the metre-gauge Attica Railways started here for Kifisia, Strofyli and Lavrio. Bus owners lobbied the line to death in 1957. No trace survives that the research found: a stop for the story only.

ilisos-open.t: The open Ilisos at Agia Fotini
p: Below the church of Agia Fotini, a short rocky bed is the last piece of the Ilisos still open. The rest of Plato's river, where Socrates sat with Phaedrus, runs 6–7 m under Kallirrois Avenue since the Metaxas government covered it in the late 1930s.
Look for two pipes where the water of the ancient Kallirroi spring still comes out. The underground channel has been damaged at Tavros since 2018.

Hadji Ali Hasekis ruled Athens brutally in the 1770s–80s; he built the city wall named after him and, in 1778, this fountain fed from the Glykotrypa springs, with double-curved arches. Ta Nea calls it the only surviving fountain of Ottoman Athens. It sits about a metre below the modern road.
Behind it, in the Agricultural University campus, his country house (konaki) keeps a vaulted ground floor and a wall fragment inside the later 'Krimbas' building.

At the east edge of the Roman Agora, a square room had seats for 64 over a channel of running water, with a gutter at their feet. Romans talked here; nobody had a cubicle. Look from the fence by the Tower of the Winds.

Found during the metro works, a section of the terracotta-lined aqueduct of the Peisistratid tyrants (6th century BC) is displayed in Evangelismos station. Other metro stations (Syntagma, Panepistimio, Dafni) show more of the city's water history.

Aggregator sites say Greece's road distances are measured from the Observatory courtyard; no physical marker has been found. The Observatory also had a noon time-ball from 1916 so the city could set its clocks. Both are leads to check on site.

A blog author reports a large, unpublished sundial (about 1 m) by the choregic monument of Thrasyllos, the cave front above the Theatre of Dionysus. Whether it is displayed or stored is unknown: a find-it detail for the south-slope walk.
A natural karst cave opens in an empty plot in Rizoupoli, surrounded by flats; newsbomb reported it in 2026. Private land: look from outside.

All that stands of the medrese (religious school) founded by Mehmet Fahri in 1721 is its marble gateway, with an Ottoman Turkish inscription of the Tulip Period, a rosette and a tulip. After independence the building became a prison where executions took place, until it was pulled down in 1915.
It stands in the shadow of Hadrian's Library and the Fethiye mosque. Read the inscription with an app: it names the benefactor and the year 1133 AH.

A short marble column about 2 m high, found near Dexameni, was a medieval marker of processions against the plague; it gave the district its name ('little column'). It was moved to the square in 1938. The square has been redesigned since and a metro station is being built: check it is still there.
At the old Rouf station on the Peloponnese line, a set of historic carriages works as a theatre, restaurant and bar. A pleasant end to a western-Athens day.

Zonar's opened in this building on 23 August 1940 (the founder Karolos Zonaras, a Greek-American, had started elsewhere in 1934 or 1939; sources disagree). For four decades it was where Athens was seen: Elytis, Gatsos, the painter Ghikas, Hadjidakis (who gave a French TV interview here with Melina Mercouri), Karezi, Kambanellis, Karamanlis; Durrell and Borges passed through.

Two of its waiters turned up in Nazi uniform in 1941, having been fifth-column spies. Seferis found it 'badly lit and vulgarly furnished'. It closed in 2001, reopened, closed again, and was renovated by K-Studio as Athénée in 2015.
The claim that Sartre and de Beauvoir 'had their table' comes from renovation PR: treat it as marketing.

Plateia Dexamenis sits on top of the reservoir built by Hadrian and still in use. At the start of the 20th century this was the 'hermitage' of Alexandros Papadiamantis, who sat here with Varnalis, Sikelianos and Souris; the famous photo of him with his head on one side was taken here, and a 1923 relief of him is set into the reservoir masonry.
Today's café is a renovated successor (reopened 2012) of the old kafeneia of Barbayiannis and 'Terpsi'. The links to Kazantzakis and Elytis are thinner; Elytis has had a statue here since 1997.

Licensed in 1915 and named after a mulberry tree, Mouria moved from a shack to a two-storey house and in 1962 into the ground floor of the block on the same corner of Charilaou Trikoupi and Kallidromiou. Plays, book launches and political meetings were held here; no famous regulars are well sourced.

In 2026 the landlord planned a pharmacy; a petition passed 7,500 signatures. In July the owner's daughter said the space would stay a café 'but we don't know if it will be Mouria'. The Mouria business is reported closed from 31 October 2026.

A family-run basement taverna since 1970. Here in 1978 Manolis Rasoulis met Nikos Xydakis, which led to 'I ekdikisi tis gyftias', one of the defining Greek albums. Savvopoulos was a regular (the owners say). A guide's claim that Seferis was 'in this house' in 1944 doesn't fit a 1970 business.

At Galaxy, top-division footballers met in 1979–80 before their first big strike, and the Panionios 'Panthers' ultras were founded one winter night in 1983. Galaxy closed in 2001 and is a municipal venue now. Adonis, made famous by Kraounakis's 1986 song sung by Protopsalti, still operates, renovated.

Down a few steps under a derelict 150-year-old house by the Central Market, Diporto has no sign and no menu: you eat what was cooked that day, among barrels, with market workers. The interior is said to be unchanged since the 1950s.
The story that Varnalis wrote 'The Moirai' here is folklore. A rumour that it was closing was denied by the co-owner.
A taverna on Plateia Theatrou since 1927, near the market, with live rebetiko and laiko. Markos and other rebetes are recorded as passing through.
The oldest tavern in Psyrri, from 1928, reopened in 2011. The rebetiko singer Tsaousakis was a regular in the early 1950s.
A Plaka distillery since 1909, now a bar whose walls of coloured bottles glow from behind. No documented famous regulars; on the map for the room.

At Votsalakia on the Kastella shore, a cave in the rock was an ancient sanctuary and bath, the Serangeion, found in 1897. In the 1920s it held a refreshment stand; by the 1960s it was the Spilia tou Paraskeva nightclub, where Manolis Chiotis and Mary Linda played and Onassis, Callas and Grace Kelly are said to have come.
The junta's mayor closed it in 1968 and it has been fenced ever since. A link with 'Never on Sunday' is claimed by one tourism site only and was not confirmed.
Stand on the shore road and look in through the fence; the Sunday stroll from Piraeus to 'the Paraskeva' is an old local habit.
A port kafeneio running since 1945, in a building owned by the Rizarios foundation; one of several old cafés of Piraeus that LiFO lists as survivors.

The American School's Gennadius Library opened in 1926 in a marble building that has not changed. It holds the archives of Seferis and Elytis and the papers of Tsatsos, Venezis, Terzakis, Myrivilis and Schliemann. No source shows Seferis worked in the reading room: this is 'sit among their papers', not 'where they sat'. The easy way in is a lecture.

The middle building of the 'trilogy' on Panepistimiou (Hansen's design, built 1887–1902) was the National Library until the move to the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Centre. Its reading room has a coffered ceiling and a five-storey cast-iron book stack in the tower behind.
The reading room has been closed since the end of 2023 for work on the ceiling; parapolitika reported it would reopen to the public in 2026. Check before going.
The new National Library in Renzo Piano's Stavros Niarchos centre: reading rooms open to anyone from 9 in the morning until midnight. Climb to the lighthouse roof for the view.

The Parnassos Literary Society's building on Plateia Karytsi has a grand hall with Roilos's painting 'The Poets'. Here Pierre de Coubertin spoke on 4 November 1894, campaigning for the first modern Olympics; Greece's first art exhibition was held under the society in 1885; in the Occupation a German military court sat here.
The society admitted its first women members only in 2023. Watch for a lecture or concert to get in.

A long low white building on Rigillis is the Athens Conservatory, designed by Ioannis Despotopoulos, who trained at the Bauhaus, as part of an unbuilt cultural centre (1959–67). Building began in 1970 and the Conservatory (founded 1871) moved in in 1977; the 600-seat amphitheatre opened only on 12 December 2022. It has been a listed modern monument since 2017.
Correction: it is often credited to Fatseas; the architect is Despotopoulos. The tree-filled garden in front is getting a €3.18 million redesign.

Built in 1836 for the Austrian diplomat Prokesch von Osten, this is one of the oldest houses outside the old town. From 1919 it housed Kalomiris's Hellenic Conservatory, where Maria Callas and Nana Mouskouri studied. It stood empty for about 50 years, burned, and in July 2022 part of its south wall collapsed onto the Ideal cinema next door.
The Culture Ministry took it over and is restoring it as the home of the Dance Archive of Greece; it was listed among the 2026 openings.

In a basement off Stadiou, Karolos Koun opened his round theatre in 1954. Here Athens first saw Beckett, Ionesco and Genet, and a generation of actors and directors learned their trade. It is still the Theatro Technis main stage; buy a ticket to sit where Koun's audience sat.
Koun's company's second stage, opened in 1985 in Plaka.

The Rex opened in 1937 as a large cinema and theatre complex; after a fire in 1982 it was listed and restored, and it is now the National Theatre's Kotopouli stage, named after the actress Marika Kotopouli.
One of the classic open-air summer cinemas, in the Zappeion gardens; its start date is given as 1903 or the late 1910s.
Since 1935, summer films on Apostolou Pavlou with the lit Acropolis behind the screen.
A Plaka roof-terrace cinema dating from the 1920s, with the Acropolis in view.
Vox on Exarchia Square dates from 1938; Riviera on Valtetsiou opened in 1969, run by the Riggas family, who also ran Vox and the Athinaia.

This is the building for a chemist. Ernst Ziller designed the University's chemistry laboratory with advice from August Wilhelm von Hofmann; at the foundation on 6 June 1887 a glass cylinder with a gold coin and a dedication 'to scientific work' was laid under it. Anastasios Christomanos founded chemistry teaching here; Carathéodory, Hondros and Zervas taught in its great amphitheatre. It burned in 1911 and was rebuilt by 1918; it also held the General Chemical Laboratory of the State and the national weights-and-measures office.

In the Occupation professor Caesar Alexopoulos hid a Telefunken transmitter by displaying it as a teaching exhibit; an antenna is still on the roof. In November 1973 the student mobilisations against the junta started here before moving to the Polytechnic.

Since 2017 it is the Law School Library (restored with SNF funds), with original benches and one laboratory preserved. Upstairs the University's Museum of Natural Sciences and Technology keeps more than 10,000 instruments, a Telefunken telegraphy collection and the archive of the University of Smyrna that Carathéodory saved in 1922. The story that Greece's national metre and kilogram copies were kept here is unproven.

In the pines of Agia Paraskevi, the Demokritos research centre's open-pool reactor, a US Atoms for Peace gift, first went critical on 27 July 1961 (the IAEA date; 31 July, often quoted, was the inauguration, when a $350,000 US grant was handed over). Greece's entry into the atomic age ran at 5 MW from 1971 and made medical isotopes such as I-131 and Tc-99m.

It is no longer operating: AthensVoice (July 2026) says it stopped in 2004 and has been in extended shutdown since, while others say a modernisation was halted in 2014; the IAEA lists it as temporarily shut down. AthensVoice was let in and reports a plan to make it a museum. Open days are the only chance to get in. The 'Turks panicked in 1977' story comes from opinion columns.
demokritos.s: IAEA Research Reactor Database; athensvoice.gr (Jul 2026); liberal.gr; en.wikipedia.

p: The Newall refractor was built in 1869 for a British amateur and for a few years was the largest in the world. It worked at Cambridge until 1957 and came to Penteli in 1959, housed in a building made entirely of Pentelic marble, with a moving floor so visitors can reach the eyepiece. Scientific use ended in the mid-1980s.
The National Observatory runs evening shows with a talk and, weather permitting, a look through the telescope.

The National Observatory's first building on the Hill of the Nymphs (Hansen, 1842), paid for by Baron Sinas; Schmidt and Eginitis worked here and Yuri Gagarin visited in February 1962. The visitor centre opens in the evenings with the historic Doridis telescope.
Leads to look for on site: the kilometre zero and the noon time-ball.

Basil Zaharoff, the Anatolian-Greek arms dealer, paid for the Hellenic Pasteur Institute, opened in March 1920 by Albert Calmette of BCG fame. Historic instruments stand in cases by the amphitheatre; groups can book tours (Friends of the Benaki have run them).
The University's mineral collection: about 1,800 specimens of over 700 mineral species in old wooden cases, plus a room on the Santorini volcano. Look for Lavrio minerals before a trip there.

In 1954 Filopimin Finos moved his company into the old Papoutsanis soap factory at Chiou 53, near Larissa station. Here the films of Greek cinema's golden age were developed, edited and mixed; the building appears in the 1966 film 'Pente chiliades psemata'. It was listed in 1986 and carries a plaque.

Film labs worked here until 2012. In July 2021 about 500 reels, including Angelopoulos's 'The Weeping Meadow', were taken out of the basement by the Greek Film Centre after a reported chemical leak (which people who knew the building denied). The building has been for sale.
Finos's stages were first at 'Atlantis' on Liosion Street, by a cement works, then from 1958 in the old Merlas stables at Agioi Anargyroi.
Karamanlis's party had its headquarters here from 1975 to 2011. The building was declared a modern monument in 2020 and a 2025 permit turns it into a private residence.

Among the spice shops of Evripidou, behind railings and trees, a single-cell chapel encloses a Roman Corinthian column whose capital pokes out of the roof. The church was built round it; a basilica here is dated to 565 by one source, and the present chapel is much later. The site is thought to have been a sanctuary of Asklepios: a mosaic floor and six ancient wells were found in 1917.

The healing tradition survived the change of god. Until the 20th century Athenians with malaria tied red and white threads to the column to bind the fever; legend said diseases were buried beneath it.

Treasure-hunt clue: find the capital above the roof among the branches, then the column inside the sanctuary. Atlas Obscura says the Eridanos runs under the church and can be heard after rain: unverified.
ag-ioannis-kolona.s: churchesingreece.blogspot (2013); Atlas Obscura; Spotted by Locals; pemptousia; avgi.

davelis-cave.t: Davelis cave and the Pentelic quarry
p: At about 700 m on the south-west face of Penteli, the ancient Spilia quarry cut so deep that it opened a cave. The quarry faces still show the ancient chisel and wedge marks, and a paved sledge path down which blocks for the Parthenon were dragged is partly preserved. In the cave mouth two small chapels, Agios Spyridon and Agios Nikolaos, are cut into the rock; their 1233–34 frescoes were moved to the Byzantine Museum in 1981.

The cave is named after Davelis, a 19th-century brigand, and has gathered legends: Pan worship, monks, Cold War tunnels. Wikipedia notes there is no evidence of Pan worship here; the shrine of Pan and the Nymphs is a smaller cave about 800 m up the slope, excavated in 1952. Military works around 1970 damaged the site.
Treasure-hunt clue: put your hand in a wedge slot. For a chemist, this is calcite marble with its famous slight iron content, which turns the Parthenon honey-coloured.
davelis-cave.s: en.wikipedia; penteli.gov.gr; odysseus.culture.gr; Google Places visitor notes.

p: Opposite the Veikou grove, the 'beautiful church' of St George is a cross-in-square of the 11th–12th century on earlier foundations, with a 13th–14th-century chapel and a later narthex. Its 13th-century frescoes include the martyrdom of St George on the wheel and a dome Pantokrator that Fotis Kontoglou called one of the most beautiful in the Christian East.

It is locked all year except on St George's day, when it fills with people. Treasure-hunt clue: a Gothic rose on the western cross-vault, a Frankish touch in a Byzantine church, and pilgrims' prayers scratched into the plaster.
omorfokklisia.s: Protothema (2024); Orthodoxia News Agency (2024); en.wikipedia; ertnews.

p: Next to the big 19th-century cathedral sits the tiny Panagia Gorgoepikoos (also Agios Eleftherios), built almost entirely of spolia: about 90 carved blocks from ancient, early Christian and middle Byzantine buildings. Its date is disputed, late 12th century or after 1436.

Treasure-hunt clue: the frieze over the west door is an ancient calendar of the Attic festivals with the signs of the zodiac, set in place as decoration. Tradition puts a temple of Eileithyia, goddess of childbirth, beneath it.

Built in the mid-11th century, Sotira Lykodimou is the largest medieval building in the city. Bavarian-era Athens sold it to Russia in 1847; it reopened as the Russian church in 1855 with a separate bell tower. A cistern of an ancient aqueduct lies 5 m below the floor: ask about it. Stories of tunnels and a temple of Apollo are weak.

In the courtyard of Hadrian's Library lie the foundations of a 5th-century tetraconch, a church with four apses (15.42 m square, by Travlos), later replaced by the Megali Panagia basilica. Clue: trace the four apses on the ground.

Above the Theatre of Dionysus, a cave in the rock face holds the chapel of Our Lady of the Golden Cave, inside the front of the choregic monument of Thrasyllos. Two columns that once held victory tripods still stand above.

The 11th-century church that sits in the middle of the shopping street was due to be demolished in the new town plan; Ludwig I of Bavaria, the king's father, intervened. Clue: inscriptions and Roman capitals on the west wall.

A UNESCO-listed 11th-century monastery on the Sacred Way to Eleusis, with gold mosaics, among them the severe Pantokrator in the dome. Cistercian monks held it under the Franks. An anchor of the Byzantine era.

In a wooded valley of Hymettus above the city, an 11th-century monastery with its bath house and refectory. Its spring, the Kallopoula, flows from a carved ram's head and was said to cure infertility.

On Mitropoleos a vaulted single-aisle church stands under the stilts of a big postwar block: Patroklos Karantinos's Ministry of Education, built over it in the 1950s. The historian Biris wrote that the chapel had been 'disfigured and humiliated' under 'an ugly building'. The ministry left in 2007 and the block has stood empty since.

Agia Dynami is linked to the War of Independence: monks are said to have made cartridges here, and a stair is said to lead to a deep room (the same story is told of the Russian Church). A tunnel to the Ilisos is legend. It keeps relics of St Nikolaos Planas, Papadiamantis's confessor.
Clue: stand inside the porch and look up; the building is the sky.

Halfway up Lycabettus, the church of Agioi Isidoroi has its sanctuary in the hill's largest cave; the living rock is behind the altar and a small spring runs from it. The church burned in 1930 and was rebuilt in 1931.

A plaque speaks of a tunnel from here to Galatsi or Penteli: legend. Next to it are the cave of St Aristides and, deeper in the rock, the 1936 shelter. Expect police tape at times; a body was found in the cave in 2026.

Leo von Klenze, Ludwig I's architect, designed this cathedral, revised by Kaftanzoglou; it was built 1853–65 and completed in 1891. Its green Tinos-marble columns were cut for the royal palace, became spare when the palace was redesigned, and came here on a French warship.
Clue for a chemist: count the columns (12 in the nave, 16 in all) and look at the green serpentinite breccia against the Pentelic floor.
The British community's church (1843), neo-Gothic in bluish-grey Hymettus marble, the stone the ancients used before they turned to white Pentelic. It has the oldest church organ in Athens.
Lysandros Kaftanzoglou's large church, begun in 1871 and finished in 1905, a monument of Greek neo-Byzantine revival in a now rough part of town.
A huge domed church on Acharnon Street, called the largest in Athens; the new church was founded in 1910 on the site of a chapel linked to a grieving mother's vow.

Karl Bensel's church for the German Evangelical community (1931–34) is the most modern religious building of interwar Athens: a plain, clear volume in the Neue Sachlichkeit manner. Inside, the pulpit, pews, candlesticks and organ gallery are original.
It is linked to the Philadelphia club, the first Goethe Institute. Go on a Sunday morning.
Across from Beth Shalom, the older synagogue of Athens's Romaniote Jews, who spoke Greek and had lived in Greece since antiquity. Visits by arrangement with the Community.
The large cathedral (1842–62) built with stone from demolished churches; it dwarfs the Little Metropolis beside it. A treasury museum opened recently. Anchor of the 19th-century era.

loumbardiaris.t: Agios Dimitrios Loumbardiaris and the Pikionis paths
p: Between the Acropolis and Philopappou, Dimitris Pikionis laid out paths, steps and resting places in 1954–58 from the debris of demolished neoclassical houses: marble door frames, roof tiles, cobbles and concrete set in patterns. At the centre stands the post-Byzantine chapel of Agios Dimitrios Loumbardiaris, which he re-clad, and a small pavilion meant as a simple café.

The name 'Loumbardiaris' comes from the Ottoman cannon (lumbarda) on the hill; legend says a lightning strike on 26 October 1656 destroyed it as it was about to fire on the faithful. Frescoes of 1735 were found inside.
The works were declared a monument in 1996. Clue: find neoclassical marble fragments reused in the paving and the walls. Pikionis turned away from his own modernist school (Pefkakia) to make this.

Sthenis Molfesis and Thymios Papagiannis designed this church in 1961, published as one of the rare modern Orthodox church designs. Whether it was built to that design is unknown: go and compare with the published plan.

Built 1956–62 to designs by Paraskevi Tsatiri with I. Theodorou, one of very few women church architects of the period. The old church was moved to make way for Vouliagmenis Avenue and kept as a chapel.

Athens was the only EU capital without an official mosque until this one opened on 2 November 2020, after decades of argument. The state built it in a former naval yard: a plain box with no minaret, for 350 men and 50 women, called an 'anti-monument'.
Most of the city's Muslims still pray in about 100 unofficial rooms in basements and garages (2017 estimate). Clue: the mihrab niche pointing to Mecca.

Opened in 1837, the First Cemetery holds the city's great and good in marble: Yannoulis Halepas's 'Sleeping Maiden', Schliemann's tomb shaped like a temple with a frieze of his excavations, prime ministers, poets and Katsimbalis, Henry Miller's 'Colossus of Maroussi'.
It climbs a hill behind the Olympic stadium; quiet, shaded, full of cats. Plan an hour.

Louis de Soissons laid out this cemetery on a gentle slope with the headstones facing the sea and no high walls. About 2,050 war dead lie here (counts vary even within the CWGC), and the Athens Memorial names some 2,870 more with no known grave.
Clue: find the different faith symbols on the stones: Gurkha and Baluchi Muslim plots, and a Crimean War plot. A designed landscape cemetery of the kind Kon likes.

Inaugurated on 28 September 1975, the cemetery at Rapendosa near Dionysos holds 9,905 German dead of the Second World War and 68 of the First, about 850 in each of 12 crypts under three walled courtyards; 843 missing are named on tablets. Among them are reportedly seven women and Moroccan soldiers.
The pines burned in 1998 and were replanted. Clue: the crypt covers in the courtyard floors. A stone path from here leads to the chapels of Agios Nikitas and Agios Loukas (lead).

Opened in 1934–36 and extended in 1942, the Third Cemetery has over 27,000 monuments and about 35,000 burials. It has a Jewish section since 1946 (vandalised), Italian Occupation, Catholic and military plots, and memorials to the Kokkinia Blockade, the Aigaleo massacre, Jewish soldiers and the Holocaust.
Clue: find the two Jewish memorials. The Blockade dead lie here; combine with the Mantra.

You know it; the point here is the details. The Parthenon has almost no straight lines: the stylobate (top step) rises about 6 cm in the middle of the short sides and 11 cm on the long sides, the columns swell slightly (entasis) and lean inwards, and the corner columns are thicker. Crouch at a corner and sight along the north or south step in low light: you can see the curve.

On 26 September 1687 a Venetian mortar fired by Morosini's army from Philopappou hit the gunpowder the Ottomans had stored in the Parthenon. About 300 people died and the middle of the temple blew out; Morosini then broke the west pediment's Poseidon group trying to take it home. The Propylaia had already been wrecked by a powder explosion in 1656, and the Ottomans dismantled the Nike temple for a gun battery.

The restorers' story is visible too. Nikolaos Balanos's iron clamps of the early 1900s rusted and split the marble; since 1975 the Acropolis Restoration Service has replaced them with titanium and filled gaps with new Pentelic marble, the bright white blocks you can spot among the honey-coloured old ones. A Mycenaean wall section is being opened to visitors.
acropolis.s: Stevens (Hesperia 1943); hh.gr; cnn.gr; Protothema (Apr 2025); History Today.

p: Closed for years, the North Slope reopened on 1 June 2025 with Onassis funding, and it is the quietest part of the Acropolis ticket. The Peripatos path circles the rock past caves: Apollo Hypoakraios with niches for votive plaques of the archons, Zeus, and Pan, whose cult came to Athens after Marathon.

Find-it details: an inscription at the foot of an upright limestone block gives the length of the Peripatos as 5 stades 18 feet; the Klepsydra spring, used since the Neolithic, seeps where porous limestone sits on impermeable schist (geology you can see); the Aglaureion, the largest cave (14 × 22 m), identified in 1980 from an inscription of 247/6 BC.
Ruins of the post-Byzantine chapel of Agios Nikolaos lie near the Pan shrine.

The theatre where Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides and Aristophanes were first staged, rebuilt in stone in the 4th century BC and refitted by the Romans. Its front row has 67 marble thrones carved with the titles of officials; the centre one belonged to the priest of Dionysus Eleuthereus (IG II² 5022).

Find-it: on the priest's throne, lion paws, satyrs and, under the inscription, two kneeling Persians holding griffins. The marble orchestra paving and the barrier round it are Nero-era, built when the theatre hosted beast shows. The open-air lapidarium has a victor's base with faint wreaths.

Below the Acropolis lay the civic centre: council house, law courts, the Tholos where the presidents dined, shops and the stoas where Socrates argued. The Hephaisteion on the hill, called the 'Theseion' since the Middle Ages, is the best-preserved temple in Greece; the Stoa of Attalos was rebuilt in 1953–56 on its original foundations and holds the museum.

Find-it: by the Tholos at the south-west corner, a marble post of about 500 BC reads, right to left, 'HOROS EIMI TES AGORAS' — 'I am the boundary of the Agora' (IG I³ 1087). A second one is under the Middle Stoa. At the Stoa of Attalos, look at its north end for original ancient blocks among the 1950s rebuild.
Upgrades (new paths, rest spots) were finished in 2026 along with Kerameikos.

roman-agora.t: Roman Agora and Tower of the Winds
p: The Tower of the Winds, built by Andronikos of Kyrrhos (2nd–mid 1st century BC), is a 12.8 m octagon of Pentelic marble. Each face carries a relief of the wind blowing from that direction, with its name. A bronze Triton weathervane once turned on top (Vitruvius describes it).

It was a scientific instrument. Under each relief are the lines of a sundial: in raking light you can read them. Inside (open since 2014–16), channels in the floor belonged to a water clock fed from an Acropolis spring, with a reservoir annex on the south side. It later served as a church and, in the 18th century, as a dervish lodge.
Next to it: the Roman latrines, the Medrese gate and the Fethiye mosque.

Kerameikos, the potters' quarter, was the city's main gate and cemetery. The Sacred Way left for Eleusis through the Sacred Gate, and the Panathenaic procession started at the Dipylon; Pericles gave his funeral speech here. The Street of Tombs keeps Classical family plots with stelai (the famous ones like Hegeso are casts; the originals are in the National Museum).

Find-it: the Eridanos stream still runs through the Sacred Gate in its stone channel, under a small arched bridge (dry in summer). On the Pompeion ramp, wheel ruts. In the lower courses of the Themistoclean Wall (479/8 BC), reused grave stelai and bases, evidence of how fast the wall was built after the Persians left.
The site reopened on 15 September 2026 after a 2023–26 upgrade with new paths and views.

Begun by the Peisistratids in the 6th century BC and finished by Hadrian in AD 132, the temple had 104 columns; 15 stand. One blew down in a storm in 1852 and lies where it fell, its drums like a sliced loaf: look at the 24 flutes and the dowel sockets.

Hadrian's Arch is free to see. Its two inscriptions face opposite ways: 'This is Athens, the old city of Theseus' and 'This is the city of Hadrian, not of Theseus'. A hermit once lived on the temple's architrave; the date of the 'stylite hut' is disputed.

On this hill the citizens of Athens met in assembly; Themistocles, Pericles and Demosthenes spoke from the rock-cut bema, about 8.35 m wide with side steps (its last phase c. 340–330 BC). The view to the Acropolis is the one they had.

Find-it: east of the bema, 58 small niches cut in the rock held votive plaques to Zeus Hypsistos, a healing god of later antiquity (Forsén 1993). Look also for the cuttings of two unfinished stoas and for the quarry marks. The astronomer Meton set up a heliotropion here in 433 BC; no trace is known.

Inventories of the 330s BC count 372 shipsheds in the harbours of Piraeus, 196 of them at Zea (today's Pasalimani). Their remains run under the modern town. At Akti Moutsopoulou and Sirangiou you can see slipways, the keel groove and column bases through the street windows of a basement, dug by Dragatsis in the 1880s.
The Zea Harbour Project found double sheds about 80 m long. This is where the fleet of Salamis was kept dry.

Rebuilt in marble for the first modern Olympics (1896) on the Roman stadium of Herodes Atticus. The vaulted tunnel under the east bank, about 57 m long, is said to be the only intact ancient part; it now leads to the Olympic torch museum. Double-faced herms at the curved end (originals or casts? check). Herodes's tomb lay on Ardettos hill above.

The hill of Ares below the Acropolis was the seat of the oldest court; tradition says St Paul preached here (Acts 17), recorded on a bronze plaque at the foot. The polished rock steps are slippery; a 2025 project reworked the plateau.

Below Parliament, a relief of a dying hoplite modelled on a figure from the Aegina temple pediment, with lines from Pericles's funeral speech and the names of battles (the list keeps growing). The Evzones change guard every hour.

In Monastiraki station (Line 3) a 24 m glass walkway crosses a 300 m² excavation where the Eridanos, Athens's buried river, still flows in its vaulted channel of Hadrian's time: 40–50 m³ an hour, about 80 after storms. Stand still and listen.
Old Line 1 signs at street level still read 'MONASTIRION' from 1895.

The metro dig at Syntagma (about 500 m²) found 35 graves, a bronze foundry, a stretch of the Eridanos bed and the Peisistratid aqueduct. A wall of the concourse shows the stratigraphy from antiquity to the 19th century, and a woman's skeleton of the 4th century BC lies in a case.

acharnian-gate.t: Acharnian Gate in the National Bank
p: When the National Bank built its new wing on Aiolou, it found the Acharnian Gate of the Themistoclean Wall and kept it: about 30 m of wall, the road through the gate with cart ruts and the moat, 5.1 m below the street, visible from the building.
A planned underground car park under Kotzia Square uncovered three ancient streets, a cemetery and workshops; the car park was abandoned and the dig left open behind railings.
At Elaionas station, the piers of an ancient bridge over the Kifisos plain are displayed: called the oldest bridge found in Greece.
The Long Walls of the 5th century BC made Athens and Piraeus one fortress. Traces survive along Thessalonikis Street, under building pilotis near Tavros station and as a tower in Moschato.

Found only in 1996 while digging for a museum, the remains of the Lyceum's palaestra mark where Aristotle taught from 335 BC, walking with his students. Modest ruins; a big name. Upgrades and digital tours were announced in 2026.

The grove of Akademos, where Plato founded his school, is a scruffy park with the remains of a gymnasium, a square peristyle and the 'Sacred House'. Few visitors; one of the most important names in philosophy.
Hadrian built a library-and-garden complex here in AD 132; its western colonnade faces Monastiraki Square. In the courtyard lie the foundations of the four-apsed early church (see Megali Panagia).

The marble temple of Poseidon (444–440 BC) stands high above the sea at the tip of Attica. It is built of local Agrileza marble from Lavreotiki, not Pentelic; four of its drums are at Chatsworth in England.

Find-it: 'BYRON' is carved on a column; that he did it himself is legend, and its position is disputed (first column on the right, lowest drum, or a south column). Visitors may not enter the temple, so bring a zoom. Dozens of 18th–19th-century travellers' names are cut beside it.

The Soros covers the 192 Athenians killed at Marathon. Schliemann dug in 1884 and found nothing; Stais found the cremation layer in 1890–91. The museum has the Ionic capital of the victory trophy and Egyptian-style statues from Herodes Atticus's sanctuary at Brexiza. The Plataean tumulus nearby was excavated in 1970.

At Brauron Athenian girls served Artemis as arktoi, 'bears'. The site keeps a stone bridge of the 420s BC with wheel grooves, the sacred spring, cave shrines and a Π-shaped stoa. Silting has moved the sea about 400 m away. The 'tomb of Iphigenia' is legend.
For two thousand years initiates walked the Sacred Way from Kerameikos to Eleusis for the Mysteries of Demeter. Today the sanctuary sits among refineries and cement works, which is part of its power.

Find-it: by the Greater Propylaea, a giant bust (probably Marcus Aurelius) from the pediment has a Christian cross scratched into the Gorgon on its breastplate. The Kallichoron well, where Demeter sat mourning, made the builders cut the lowest Propylaea step short. The Ploutonion cave, the door to the underworld, is behind.
An abandoned junction of the dead Peloponnese metre-gauge network with rusting trains on its sidings, about 2 hours from Athens.
Unverified since 2018; check recent photos before going.
The family house of the inventor of the Pap test, now a museum, about 2 hours from Athens.
Short hours (e.g. Tue and Thu evenings, Sat morning); check before going.
An 'almost anti-plastic' modern chapel built in 1960 by the architect Giannakis on the summit of Kithairon during his military service, near the old NIKE flight.
Lead, not verified; mountain access.
Greece's first crematorium (30 Sept 2019), by MONOGON architects, about 80 km from Athens; the end of a long religious and legal fight.
Working crematorium; exterior.

Papagou is a planned suburb, not a village that grew. The Autonomous Building Organisation of Officers (AOOA) was set up on 29 August 1950; King Paul laid the first house in early 1952 with Prime Minister Plastiras present, and the first 200 houses were handed out by lottery on 22 June 1954. Walk its quiet streets, named after fallen officers, and look for low, plain houses with pitched roofs among the newer villas.

The architect Achilleas Spanoudis designed the house types and the building programmes for over thirty years (1950–82): eleven programmes in six zones, with 18 parks and 13 squares. The first-period type (1952–69) has been studied in a university thesis, which is the best guide to which houses are still original. Zone 1 (1952–54) is where to start.

Papagou was part of Cholargos until 1965 and still feels like a state project: a Cold War suburb for the officer class, a few hundred metres from the 'Pentagon'. The story that the Beatles stayed here for a few days is unverified.
papagou-garden.s: dpapxol.gov.gr; amarysia.gr; UNIWA thesis on the AOOA house type. Map pin approximate.

ieta-mint.t: Bank of Greece banknote works (IETA), Mesogeion 341
p: Behind the fence on Mesogeion stands the Bank of Greece's printing works and mint: a long, plain building in a Π shape, designed by K. Papadakis and A. Delendas and refined by a specialist from the Austrian state printing works. It was finished in early 1941, just in time to be requisitioned by the German Aegean admiralty.

So the first note came only in 1947, a brown 1,000 drachmas with Kolokotronis; coins followed from 1972. The basement has a four-chamber air-raid shelter for 300 people. The plot of 214.5 stremmata was a former estate mortgaged to the Bank in 1937.
Even the Bank cannot decide where it is: one of its pages puts it in Halandri, another in Cholargos.

The huge complex on Mesogeion is the seat of the Greek general staffs, known to everyone as the 'Pentagon'. It is not five-sided: an army document only called the building 'idiomorphic'. Today it wears a new façade and Varotsos's sculpture 'Ark of National Memory'.

Construction began in October 1951 with Marshall-plan credits, for a hospital. The Army General Staff moved in on 22 May 1955, as Greece settled into NATO. Sources give 1950, 1951 or 1952 for the start; 1951 is the best supported.

psychiko-plan.t: Old Psychiko: the 1923 plan and the First Square
p: Old Psychiko looks like no other part of Athens because a company drew it. The KEKROPS company was founded in 1923 and Alexandros Nikoloudis drew the plan, approved on 17 July 1923: streets 15–20 m wide ending in circular squares, with the company building the roads and utilities itself. The 1923 decree made every block residential-only, and it still holds: in 2024–25 the planning council ruled against a hotel here.

Start at the First Square (Α' Πλατεία). The corner building is the former Blue Bell, opened in March 1968 for the 'golden youth', with a phone on every table (the 'first in Greece' claim is nostalgia); it is now a post office and a municipal hall. From there walk the listed houses: Lymperopoulou, 25is Martiou, Ag. Dimitriou, Antheon and Vas. Pavlou. Most of the 1930s modernist villas by Vourekas, Kapsambelis and others have been demolished, so the survivors matter.

Political Psychiko is on the same streets: at Gyzi 58 Andreas Papandreou was arrested at dawn on 21 April 1967 (a 1934 house; no plaque, and whether it still stands is unchecked). Kosmas Politis's house at Strat. Kallari 13 became the town hall in 1987, and the Bodosakis house was left to the state as a presidential residence. On Dafnis St a grove has carried a marble inscription since 2024 for 'Pat' of Force 133, a resistance agent.

The 'first private plan in Greece' label is shaky: a 1908 decree had already approved a street plan here. The company's drawings also showed a theatre, skating rink and casino that were never built, and the municipality says KEKROPS later sold off common land for profit.
psychiko-plan.s: philothei-psychiko.gov.gr; newmoney.gr; ethnos.gr; archetype.gr (DOCOMOMO survey 2019); athensmagazine.gr; tovima.gr. Map pin approximate.

filothei-garden.t: Filothei garden city: Siadima Square and the Kremezis houses
p: Filothei was founded in January 1929 by a National Bank staff cooperative on what the founders called 'a barren rocky waste 8 km from Athens'. The bank's engineer N. Zoumboulides drew the plan; Ioannis Kremezis, just graduated, won the call for house types in 1931; the foundation stone was laid on 6 February 1933. Siadima Square is one of the planned squares and a good place to read the layout.

Two thirds of the land were kept for common use, with only two small markets allowed, and 28,000 trees were planted in the first two years (Poulakis grove carries the name of the man who supervised it). The cooperative was wound up in 1971. Which original Kremezis houses survive is still open: a 2026 municipal survey recorded 3,531 historic buildings from 1924–70.

The stone U-plan building at the heart of Athens College is the Benakeio, designed by K. Sgoutas, K. Kyriakidis and G. Soulis. Its academic eclectic façades were simplified at the board's request. The east wing went up in 1927–29 and the west wing after the war; Venizelos opened it in 1929.

Classes started on 12 November 1928, among the builders, after a dengue epidemic delayed the opening. The TEE heritage register calls it the first modern, fully equipped private school building in Attica. It was damaged during the German occupation.

arsakeio.t: Arsakeio Psychiko and the Agia Anastasia chapel
p: The Arsakeio moved its girls' school out of downtown Athens to this hillside: foundation laid on 23 July 1931, built by 1933 to a design by Kriezis, chosen over a team that included the Swiss Boudet and Vincent and the Frenchman Lefèvre. It had boarding for 150 girls. In the grounds stands the domed cross-in-square chapel of Agia Anastasia (1935), also by Kriezis.
During the war the school was requisitioned as a hospital. A floor was added after 1987. Kossos's bust of the benefactor Arsakis was moved here from the old downtown building in 1935.

This is the house-workshop of the ceramicist Panos Valsamakis, not of the architect Nikos Valsamakis, though the mix-up is easy. It is a two-level 1965 house designed for working and living at once, beside Kifisias Avenue in Paradisos, Marousi, and was listed for Open House Athens in 2025.
Unlike most modernist houses on this map you can go in: the family gives tours of the 1960s home and studio, and runs a workshop where you glaze your own tile.

The villa at Plateia Kennedy was listed in 1999 and then abandoned until it was close to collapse. In 2020 the municipality intervened and plans a public garden of 2.7 stremmata around it. A local councillor counted it as the last of its kind after the Prapopoulou villa was lost.
Plateia Kennedy was also a halt on the Lavrio railway, between Gerakas and Halandri; nothing of it has been found. Doukissis Plakentias metro sits on the old line but was never a stop.

At Sof. Venizelou 68 and Salaminos stood the interwar Douzeni distillery, registered in 1939 and listed in 1999. On 15 August 2005, a holiday when no one was watching, the owner bulldozed it. On 4 July 2025 the council voted unanimously to buy the 3-stremma plot in instalments, at €550 per m², for culture and green space.

It was the last trace of the industrial Kato Halandri around Marmariotissa. The municipality says marble cutters settled here for the underground water; a big marble works called 'Akropolis' gave its name to a bus stop. The tale that the Parthenon's blocks were split here is local legend.
douzeni.s: chalandri.gr (council notices 2025); amarysia.gr; vidarchives.gr. Map pin approximate.

p: Behind Psychiko the Tourkovounia hills end in cliffs: the abandoned quarries of LATO and KEKROPS, a basin of about 500 stremmata with half-collapsed industrial buildings, a working Agios Savvas chapel, a small goat farm and graffiti. Walk in from the Galatsi side for the full view of the cut faces.

The irony is the point. KEKROPS, the company that built the Psychiko garden suburb, acquired the hillside in 1927 and quarried it; LAPSY merged with it in 1952, LATO extended the workings into Galatsi from 1949, and quarrying went on until a 1976 law banned it. A suit filed in 1988 ended only in 2022, when the Supreme Court recognised the state as owner of 242 stremmata. At least three university theses propose turning it into a park.
The junta planned a huge 'National Votive' church of the Saviour on the Tourkovounia; it was never built. G1 wrote 'LAPSY' for the second quarry; the names on the ground are LATO and KEKROPS.
tourkovounia-quarries.s: el.wikipedia (Tourkovounia); top-nea.gr (Lavda, 2022); philothei-psychiko.gov.gr (2026); TUC and NTUA theses.

lavrio-rails-filothei.t: Lavrio-line rails and bridge, Lavriou St
p: In the median of Lavriou Street, on the border of Agia Filothei and Alsoupoli, the metre-gauge rails of the Athens–Lavrio railway are still in the ground, with a small railway bridge intact. Most other stretches were destroyed for the 2004 Olympic works, so this is the place to see the line itself.

The line ran from Lavrio Square in central Athens out through Irakleio, Agia Filothei, Halandri and Gerakas to the mines. The Athens–Strofyli branch opened on 4 February 1885; passenger service on the Lavrio line was suspended in 1957 and it closed for good in 1962. The Germans used it in the occupation for the Kalogreza mines nearby, according to Wikipedia.
lavrio-rails-filothei.s: el.wikipedia (Lavrio–Agioi Anargyroi line; Alsoupoli); ertnews.gr; NTUA Attica Rail Trail. Map pin approximate.

halandri-station.t: Old Halandri station, now a children's library
p: The small station building at Palaiologou, Averof and Solonos served Halandri on the Lavrio railway, which reached here in 1885. Since 2005 it has been the 'Mimis Vasilopoulos' children's library, renovated as a gift of the Evripidis bookshops. In the median of Palaiologou and Papanikoli metre-gauge rails still show in places, continuing as Kapodistriou St in Filothei.

Whether the building is the 1885 original is unproven: one enthusiast page says the first station was demolished before 1975. The bus stop 'Sidera' (the irons) on Kifisias near Zalokosta keeps the memory of the level crossing; residents remember an iron arched bridge removed around 1974 for the interchange, which is unverified.
The Athens–Strofyli line opened on 4 February 1885 and the section closed on 8 August 1938 (en.wikipedia); passenger trains on the wider Lavrio line ran until 1957.
halandri-station.s: chalandri.gr; el.wikipedia; en.wikipedia (Lavrio Sq.–Strofyli railway); dtert.gr.

p: At the Kifisias–Kapodistriou interchange stood the Rotonda, a circular glass café-restaurant of 1934 with dance orchestras, one of the Filothei cooperative's first buildings and probably designed by Kremezis. It became the template for kiosk-cafés all over Greece. It was demolished and its park paved for the flyover: athensvoice.gr says in the 1960s, a 2026 blog says the late 1970s.
rotonda-site.s: archetype.gr (Exarchopoulos 2019); athensvoice.gr; exnet.gr. Map pin approximate.

anastasi-six.t: Anastasi 'of the Six': the 1922 execution ground and chapel
p: In this pine grove on the Cholargos–Papagou border, at 11:30 on 15 November 1922, the former prime minister Dimitrios Gounaris and five others were executed after the 'Trial of the Six', blamed for the Asia Minor disaster. They are buried in the First Cemetery; the stones in the grove are memorials. The small chapel of the Resurrection (Anastasi) was built for them.

The chapel was paid for by a 1934–35 public subscription in the newspapers Kathimerini and Vradyni. Prime Minister Tsaldaris laid the foundation stone in November 1935; Anastasios Orlandos designed it in Byzantine style and it was finished at the end of 1937, painted by Dimitrios Pelekasis and completed inside in July 1940. No inscription says why it was built.

A greekarchitects.gr essay describes a 1968 church here in bare concrete, clay pipes and glass, set apart from older walls by a deep groove and compared to Niemeyer's Pampulha chapel. That is not the chapel: most likely it is the Ypsosi Timiou Stavrou parish church in the same grove, which now owns the park. Its architect is still unknown, so look for the groove yourself.
anastasi-six.s: vimaorthodoxias.gr; orthodoxianewsagency.gr (2022); ertnews.gr; greekarchitects.gr; menoumeholargo.gr. Pin at the parish church in the grove.

saligaros-villa.t: Saligaros villa: Italian HQ, now the photo archive
p: The villa at Aetideon and Polymnias belonged to Nikolaos and Pasithea Saligaros, among the founders of Cholargos, which began in 1930 as a farm cooperative's country retreat. In 1940–41 the Italians took it as their occupation headquarters.

Today it belongs to the municipality and holds the historical photo archive; a visitor describes a photographic exhibition of 20th-century Cholargos inside. It is one of the last country villas of the early suburb.

tourkovounia-1944.t: Mass grave of 45 patriots, Tourkovounia saddle (1944)
p: On the saddle of the Tourkovounia, three broken marble crosses and a small metal shrine stand on open ground. One cross reads: 'Mass grave of 45 patriots executed by the Germans on 29 September 1944.' Oral history collected in Galatsi says the Germans rounded up the men they found and shot them here; among them was Mitsos Avouris, communist party secretary of Ampelokipi.

On 24 October 2017 the Galatsi municipality unveiled a marble stele at Protopapadaki and Kalpakiou listing nine named victims, one of them 'Asvestas Nikolaos, aged 16'. Whether it stands at the crosses or separately is not confirmed, and the count of 45 may include burials from December 1944. Which municipality the site lies in is unclear too.
tourkovounia-1944.s: efsyn.gr (2017); e-galatsi.gr (Athens Oral History Group); galatsi.gov.gr. Map pin approximate.

p: This 1923 villa, built for a Greek-Cypriot businessman, was bought in 1937 by King George II for his brother Paul and Frederica. Princess Sofia (1938) and Constantine II (1940) were born here. After 1974 the state took it; it was sold to the Chatziioannou family and is now a rebuilt beige mansion, so what you see is new.

neo-psychiko-fountain.t: Refugee fountain, Agios Georgios Square, Neo Psychiko
p: Neo Psychiko began not as a garden city but as a refugee and civil-servant settlement, first counted in the 1929 census; 60–70 families came from shacks on monastery land along the railway. The fountain on Agios Georgios Square carries the names of the Asia Minor villages they left.

The church of Agios Georgios was first a mud-brick building of 1932 for refugees from Vourla, who brought an icon of 1850; it was extended, rebuilt in 1956–57 and finally replaced by today's large church. Compare this square with Old Psychiko's round ones a kilometre away.

halandri-square.t: Halandri central square, Agios Nikolaos and the heroon
p: Below Agios Nikolaos, Halandri's central church, is the square that was the village. The heroon (war memorial) stands on the site of four large halls built in 1910 for an agricultural and beekeeping school. A 1928 photo shows Kanaris's kafeneio on the square.

Between the wars Halandri was where Athenians went for summer air: the municipality lists the tavernas Adam, Ginis, Boem, Heraio, Ivi, Remvi and Farida, all gone. Refugees from Smyrna and Çeşme arrived in 1926–27, about 900 people in a town of 6,000. The name 'Halandri' has three rival etymologies (a landowner Halas, a Byzantine word for a monk's cell, Turkish 'uncle's stream'); none is proven.

The Rematia is a real stream running through the suburbs from Penteli, protected since 1995 by presidential decree (ΦΕΚ 659/Δ/95). Paths follow it under plane trees past bridges of 1947 (Gyftopoulou St) and 1957 (Varnali St) and a stone bridge on Asklipiou St. The open-air theatre of 1981 burned in 2015 and was rebuilt within a month; it hosts summer concerts.

About 150 plant species grow here and the municipality's walking map says the bird list 'tops 60 species', including the established ring-necked parakeets. The water table lies 2–10 m down. During the occupation the Germans fenced and mined the ravine as an ammunition store.

Watch the stream disappear: at Solomou St it enters a culvert that drains to the Podoniftis and the Kifisos; Attiki Odos buried another part. In 1934–36 62 small stone houses were built on its banks for refugee families, after about 5,000 refugees of 1928 had lived for ten years in shacks and tents; whether any survive is unknown. A 2009–10 dig found the ancient road that carried Pentelic marble to the Acropolis alongside it, probably backfilled.
rematia.s: chalandri.gr (Rematia map and PDF, Sosrematia); topoguide.gr; ertnews.gr.

p: George Zongolopoulos (1903–2004) and the painter Eleni Paschalidou lived and worked in this house for more than sixty years. The studio in the yard still has his tools and materials; the Foundation, set up in the year he died, keeps over a thousand works, a library and an archive. It is free and quiet, and you can walk in on a weekday.

Down Dimokratias, on the square named after him beside Agios Dimitrios, an open-air gallery shows seven large works lent with the collector Zacharias Portalakis.
