His 'Umbrellas' mark the Psychiko entrance on Kifisias Avenue. More than 30 public sculptures are scattered round the municipality, including Afroditi Liti's 'Pine cone' at the Second Square.

Alekos Kontopoulos (1904–1975), a painter who moved from realism to abstraction and fought in the Resistance, lived in this house from 1967 until his death. The museum, opened in 1999 inside the municipal library, keeps his sitting room and studio. The plot was donated by Marcelle Kontopoulou.

The house was left to the town by the teacher Kalliopi Moustaka-Aetopoulou and has run as a cultural centre since 1982, with the municipal library and a store of local antiquities. It published Loukas's 'Phlya' (1990), the key history of the ancient deme under Halandri, and runs the Rematia Theatre.

agia-paraskevi-square.t: Agia Paraskevi square and Cine Amaryllis
p: Agia Paraskevi grew around a pilgrimage chapel on this empty land, which nine Halandri men bought from Count Antonios Botsaris in 1850; the feast on 26 July still fills the square. The Amaryllis summer cinema was built when the square was bare earth; it started with 800 seats under Giannis Stefos, later shrank, and is listed. It says 'since 1923' (Athens Voice), cinema-history sources say 1935; new operators took over in 2018.

The parish church was founded in 1934; when the old chapel was demolished in 1937, its altar area was kept. Find it. The heroon on the square is a geometric composition, possibly mid-century modernist; its architect is unknown.
Before 1948 the area drew tuberculosis patients, who rented or built shacks in the vineyards for the air. The first house, Davaris's, dates from 1894.

cine-psychiko.t: Cine Psychiko and the lost Faros light
p: The Faros (lighthouse) stop on Kifisias is named after a night traffic light on a tall concrete column at the junction with the old Halandri road. On 31 March 1933 the shipowner Achilleas Mantakas, owner of the 'Mega Ethnikon' hotel, drove into it and died; it was never put back.

Cine Psychiko started with about 1,000 seats among pine trees: the cineanamnisi blog dates it to 1941 from a newspaper of 23 February 1941, urbanlife.gr to 1943. It was rebuilt inside a new complex in the 2000s and now has a roof bar.

marmariotissa.t: Panagia Marmariotissa: a Roman tomb that became a church
p: Behind the new parish church of Panagia Marmariotissa sits a small, low building of Pentelic marble with its floor several metres below today's street. It is a Roman mausoleum, dated by de-facto.gr to the 2nd to mid-3rd century AD (the Byzantine monuments database says late Roman to early Byzantine), converted into a church. It is the oldest roofed building near Halandri.

Find-it: the barrel vault of marble voussoirs, and the entrance. The tomb's door was on the east, where the three-sided apse is now; you enter from the west. Inside are fragments of 17th-century frescoes, on which Anastasios Orlandos read an incised date of 1717.

Rey and Chenavard drew it in 1867 as 'Tombeau de Kalandri', useful for a then-and-now comparison. The link to Herodes Atticus's circle rests only on its likeness to the Kifisia tomb, and 'the oldest building in Attica still in use' is local pride, not fact.

Above Papagou, on the west slope of Hymettus, a cross-in-square church with an Athenian-type dome stands inside a walled enclosure with a post-Byzantine tower, a refectory and a garden kept by the nuns. The view takes in the whole basin.

It is a dating puzzle you can stand inside. A 1921 royal decree declared it an outstanding Byzantine monument; the Byzantine Monuments of Attica database now dates it to the 15th–17th century, and lists Krautheimer at about 1120, Chatzidakis after the 12th century, Orlandos 13th–14th and Sotiriou 16th–17th. Kambouroglou wrote that 'we know almost nothing'. Look at the tower and the narthex joint and decide.

It became a dependency of the Petraki monastery in 1702, a women's hesychasterion in 1942 and a convent in 1971. The claims of a temple of Artemis on the site and of St Basil studying here are tradition.

kynigos.t: Moni Agiou Ioanni Kynigou (Monastery of the Philosophers)
p: At the north end of Hymettus, above Agia Paraskevi, the monastery of St John 'the Hunter' looks east over the Mesogeia. It was founded in the 12th century and is mentioned by Michael Choniates in 1207; the founder's tomb slab of 1235 is in the Byzantine Museum, and an inscription recorded a road built in 1238. The Metropolis's history quotes a 1205 inscription naming a 'philosopher monk', hence 'of the Philosophers'.

Abbot Basil dedicated it to John the Baptist and his nephew Loukas 'the Kynigos' (hunter) succeeded him in the early 13th century. It was dissolved in 1837 and refounded as a convent in 1975. In the 1920s Kazantzakis planned a spiritual commune here. The 10th-century foundation date sometimes quoted is weakly argued.
Good start for mountain-bike and walking tracks on Hymettus; the road up has no pavements.

frangoklisia.t: Frangoklisia: the vanished Frankish chapel, Ano Halandri
p: The neighbourhood name Frangoklisia ('Frankish church') remembers a real building. A rescue dig at the junction of Pentelis Avenue and Attiki Odos found a 13th-century single-nave chapel with a later narthex, published by A. Pantelidou in Archaiologikon Deltion 56–59. It was detached and moved to a plot at Attikis × Lefkon Oreon; a resident says the remaining marbles lie dumped on a pavement 200 m east.

Whether it was really 'Frankish' (Latin) is not shown; the town's historic map calls it a small Byzantine church, and old maps mark 'Frangomonastiro'. Do not confuse it with the Fragoklisia at Vagiati on Penteli. Treat this as a hunt, and report back.
frangoklisia.s: kourelis.blogspot.com (ADelt 56–59, 2011); sarantakos.wordpress.com; chalandri.gr historic map. Map pin approximate.

p: The parish church of Old Psychiko was built in 1929–30 by the engineer Th. Kyriakidis to a design by Anastasios Orlandos, the great restorer of Byzantine churches: a cross-in-square with a dome. The bell tower (1956), two colonnaded stoas (1962), a fountain by G. Dimopoulos and a chapel (1986) came later; Pelekasis and Malamas painted the icons.

Find-it: on the north side near the templon, a baroque icon stand made in Constantinople carries the inscription 'Offering of Elika Athanasiadou'. The priest says her bones are said ('legetai') to lie in it; treat that as a story. A tiny chapel of Ai-Dimitris stood here before 1929.
Zongolopoulos's open-air sculpture gallery is on the square next door.

filothei-crypt.t: Crypt and church of Agia Filothei
p: On a pine-covered hill of red stone, a small natural cave has been made into a chapel: the crypt said to be the 16th-century prayer place of Rigoula Benizelou, St Filothei of Athens. Above it stands a small church by Nikolaos Zoumboulides, one of Filothei's first residents, opened on 25 March 1937 and only formally consecrated on 13 May 2017, 'after 80 years of delays'.

The official story says quarrymen cutting red stone for the new houses found the cave by chance in 1934. The historian E. Skiadas shows a 1922 photograph of it by D. Chatzopoulos, and quarrying in the 1920s threatened to blast it until the ephor G. Sotiriou withdrew the licence. 1934 is when the new community and the Society of Athenians began to promote it; the find renamed the settlement from 'Nea Alexandreia' to Filothei.
The tunnel through which the nuns supposedly escaped to Kalogreza is folklore. So is the story that Psychiko is named after St Filothei's charitable well.

The first Agia Sofia, named for Queen Sophia and designed by Iph. Kokkidis, was built in 1929–33 and first used on 18 March 1937. The present church was founded on 22 October 1961 and finished in 1967, with Onassis among the donors; frescoes by the Balogiannis brothers followed in 1970–98.

Its architect was the academician Solon Kydoniatis, according to the first priest's own account and Wikipedia's list of his works; the municipality and the parish text say 'Athanasios', which looks like a mistake. The square in front, with its fountain and pergolas, is Neo Psychiko's sitting room.

catholic-john-psychiko.t: Catholic church of St John the Baptist, Psychiko
p: The complex at Papanastasiou 11 was first an Institute of Byzantine Studies run by the Assumptionist Fathers. It became a parish in 1968 (the first church is now the parish hall), was recognised in 1972, and got its present church in 1978. It is one of very few non-Orthodox churches in the northern suburbs, used today by an international congregation.

Halandri's cemetery, with its chapel of the Archangel Michael at Anapafseos and Tinou, holds the comic actor Sotiris Moustakas, the actress Maria Boneloy, the director Giorgos Lazaridis, the fashion designer Sophia Kokosalaki, Takis Vougiouklakis, and the actress Chrysa Spilioti, a victim of the 2018 Mati fire. Burial priority goes to Halandri residents.

papagou-cemetery.t: Papagou cemetery and the Hymettus track
p: The Papagou and Cholargos cemeteries lie side by side at the end of Anastaseos St, at the edge of Hymettus and close to the Theologos convent. Opposite, just past the forest barrier, the dirt road has an informal pet cemetery that has been there 'for many years'. Keep walking: it is the shortest way onto Hymettus from Cholargos, with views over the whole basin to the Acropolis and Piraeus.

Konstantinos Karamanlis, who restored democracy in 1974, died on 23 April 1998 and is buried in the courtyard of his foundation, set up in 1983 as an archive and research centre. Visitors report that the grave can be seen during opening hours; a memorial service is held every April. The municipality has no cemetery of its own that could be found.

tourkovounia-peak.t: Tourkovounia north peak: Zeus's altar on Anchesmos
p: The north peak of the Tourkovounia (304 m) keeps traces of an ancient altar, beacon or statue base, photographed in 1932, 1978 and 2016 and published as early as 1920. It is probably Pausanias's Anchesmos with its statue of Zeus Anchesmios; Galatsi frames it as a rain cult of Zeus Ombrios. Finds are reported to be in the Kifisia archaeological collection.

On the way down you pass the Lato quarries, a lime kiln and the 'Spiral'. The view runs from Aigaleo, Parnitha, Penteli and Hymettus to Salamis and Aegina; rare wildflowers grow on top. The 19th-century brigand Kakaras is said to have hidden in these hills, which is folklore.
tourkovounia-peak.s: philothei-psychiko.gov.gr; galatsi.gov.gr; viewsofgreece.gr. Map pin approximate.

p: At the east end of the Elefsina seafront stands the Kronos distillery: concrete halls with mushroom columns and vaults, and two distillation towers that look, as one writer put it, like an interwar mansion. The industrial archaeologist Nikos Belavilas rates it the most important industrial monument of the area: the buildings survive whole, the machinery does not.

The company was founded in 1922 and the plant worked from 1926; its reinforced-concrete structures were designed by Pavlos Santorinis and built by Tekton S.A., and it employed about 300 people. It closed in the 1980s, was bought by a shipowner in 1991, hosted exhibitions and the Aischyleia festival in 2003–05, and has stood shut since. Only the distillery tower and the administration building are listed (1990).

Its future is unclear. One report says the government bought it for the municipality from a 2023 grant and the council approved the purchase; that could not be confirmed, and in 2025 the Kronos jetty was being used to park tankers. Look from outside the fence.
kronos.s: TUC thesis on Kronos; Kathimerini via parianostypos.gr; elefsina.gr; healthyliving.gr (Belavilas); hellenicparliament.gr (2025). Map pin approximate.

iris-elefsina.t: IRIS paint works and its chimney, Elefsina
p: IRIS made oil paints, varnishes, ship-hull paint and printing inks from 1925. Its listed buildings and the tall brick chimney, the 'Kaminada', were restored for the 2023 European Capital of Culture. In front of it the Elaiourgiki, a single interwar hall of about 900 m² (the SYNPE olive-oil plant), was used for workshops in 2023.
Since the Old Oil Mill was handed to the ministry for a museum, the Aischyleia festival performs here; regulars complain about the seats.

elaiourgeio.t: Old Oil Mill and Votrys soap works, Elefsina
p: The Charilaou soap works of 1875 was Elefsina's first factory, built right next to the ancient sanctuary; later it became the Old Oil Mill, and its yard hosted the Aischyleia festival in a 2,000-seat open-air theatre. Two buildings of the Votrys soap works and two chimneys were listed in 2008.

The Ministry of Culture plans the Diachronic Museum of Elefsina here, with 3,800 m² of galleries, so expect works. Elefsina's industry went from soap and spirits (Kronos) to paint (IRIS), cement (Titan, 1902) and steel (Halyvourgiki, from 1951): the seafront is a timeline.

titan-elefsina.t: Titan cement works and the lost Cave of Pan
p: The Titan cement plant opened in 1902; Belavilas calls it Elefsina's industrial leap. It also shows what industry cost: the Cave of Pan, 45 m up the western hill and reached through a cleft 0.8 m wide, was quarried away by Titan in 1931. Only a relief survives.
titan-elefsina.s: academia.edu (Belavilas et al.); proseleusis.com; gowestathens.gr. Map pin approximate.

elefsina-airbase.t: Elefsina air base and the 1941 airmen
p: In April 1941 the last 15 RAF Hurricanes in Greece were based here. On 20 April Squadron Leader Pat Pattle was shot down into Elefsina Bay. The Luftwaffe held the base from 26 April; USAAF raids followed, among them 109 B-17s on 20 December 1943. A memorial to the fallen airmen of 1940–41 and an RAFA memorial in town host an annual remembrance; the town memorial's exact spot is unconfirmed.
elefsina-airbase.s: skai.gr; thriassio.gr; elefsina.gr; tovima.gr. Map pin approximate.

p: In a back street of Megara lies the fountain house of the tyrant Theagenes, of the first quarter of the 5th century BC: 21 m long, holding 350 m³. The Herakleidon Museum calls it the largest found in Greece so far. It has two chambers fed separately, so one half could be emptied and cleaned while the other kept running; one inlet still shows traces of a bronze flow regulator. Eleven poros pillars stood in front; none survive. The German Archaeological Institute dug it in December 1899.

The water came through the Orkos underground aqueduct, a network of tunnels with surface shafts on four axes, which locals call 'Eupalinos's aqueduct' after the Megarian engineer of the Samos tunnel. It was in use until 1935 and excavation began in 2011; the shafts are visible in the fields, the tunnels are closed.

Megara's museum (closed Tuesday) stands before a cave thought to have been Demeter's. On Easter Tuesday the women dance the Trata in costume at Agios Ioannis Galilaios square; the claim that it is unbroken from antiquity has no evidence.

Megara's old station is a group of 1885 buildings on 13,705 m² of the Piraeus–Peloponnese metre-gauge railway, with an old steam locomotive on display. Trains ran until about 2005, and the station is the start point of Railbiking tours on the abandoned line to Kakia Skala.

It is not going to stay a ruin: as 'Palaios SS Megaron' it becomes the terminus of the new West Attica suburban line from Ano Liosia (8 stations, on the old corridor), forecast for late 2026 or early 2027.

vourkari.t: Vourkari wetland and the 1821 wall, Megara
p: Vourkari is a coastal wetland of about 178 ha between Nea Peramos and Pachi, protected since 2017. Its management plan records 222 bird species; flamingos and little egrets are there all year, and a 2010 winter count found 8,600 Mediterranean gulls. It has shrunk from about 5 km² to about 1 km².

Next to it the Agia Triada wall began in 1818 as a farm wall built with the Ottoman pass-guard's permission and was turned into a fortification in 1821. Nearby Megara–Pachi airfield is where British paratroops dropped in October 1944, with many jump injuries.

kakia-skala.t: Kakia Skala: German posts on the abandoned cliff railway
p: Between Megara and Kineta the old road and the metre-gauge railway cling to the cliffs of Kakia Skala, the Skironian Rocks where Theseus threw the robber Skiron into the sea. The line, built in the 1880s and used until the late 1990s, is abandoned and in many places looted; a 2025 walking route follows it for about 7.5 km each way, starting at the derelict Stika lime kiln.

Along it the Germans built at least five posts within about 880 m, with Megarians as forced labour: pillboxes on both sides of a railway bridge, one visibly damaged, and the bridge they blew up nearby (an 1885 photo shows the original iron one). They are unsigned and hard to see from the road.
The new standard-gauge line runs in tunnels named Skiron, Theseus, Aithra and Eupalinos; do not enter them.
kakia-skala.s: fortifications.gr; mixanitouxronou.gr; efsyn.gr; el.wikiloc.com; travel.gr. Map pin approximate.

p: On the north-east slopes of Gerania, above the Megara plain, the monastery of Agios Ierotheos has a pomegranate tree growing on the saint's tomb, a 15th-century vaulted monument of the Kyparissiotissa recalling the monks' escape from pirates, and a bell tower on ancient or early Christian columns.

In 1941–44 British soldiers hid nearby, and the monastery holds the National Resistance Medal. Sources disagree on the details: twenty men in a neighbouring cave, or eighteen, ten of them in an abandoned wine press (G. Saliagkakis, Nov 2026). Ask the nuns.

Gyftokastro is one of the best-preserved fortresses in Greece: an 860 m circuit of mortarless walls 2.6 m thick with twelve towers, two main gates and four small ones, on a ridge over the Kaza pass. Find the stone stairs inside the walls that climb to the wall-walk; Pomardi drew it in 1804–05 as 'Oenoe or Ghiftocastro'.

Who built it is still argued: Athens or Thebes, both wanted this pass. Its last building phase is 7th century AD, and two early Christian basilicas sit on the rocky ridge to the east. The name, 'Gypsies' castle', comes from Roma who lived there in late Byzantine or early Ottoman times.
It is the anchor of a chain of frontier towers: Oinoe tower down the road, the Vathychori towers on Pateras and Aigosthena on the gulf.
gyftokastro.s: athensattica.com; el.wikipedia; topoguide.gr; photodentro.edu.gr. Map pin approximate.

p: A lone square tower on the road to Boeotia, with a later building phase of the mid-4th century BC; part of the system of towers that watched the Attic frontier alongside Gyftokastro.

On the south-east slope of Pastra above Oinoi, at 520 m, the monastery of Osios Meletios keeps a 12th-century katholikon: a composite four-column cross-in-square, probably built over an older church, with 16th-century frescoes. The saint died in 1105; his skull is in the crypt on the north side.

Find-its: the 12th-century Taxiarches chapel attached on the south-west, and ancient blocks said to come from ancient Myoupolis. The monastery was dissolved in 1833 and has been a nunnery since about 1949–50.

vilia.t: Vilia: the square, the mills and the road to Kithairon
p: Vilia is where Athenians come on winter Sundays for grilled meat by the fire: Elatos, a music kafeneio with rakomelo, and Opos Palia face the square, with Ernst Ziller's Metamorfosi church of 1893 and the post-Byzantine Taxiarches of 1637.

Below the village the Goura spring drove five watermills, three in a row below a chapel; the 1889 industrial survey lists them, and they stopped around 1918 when a steam mill opened. Trail O22 passes them on the way to the Tsakos refuge (2 h) and the Kithairon summit (about 5 h return); another old mule path, 2.4 m wide so two loaded mules could pass, runs from Agios Nektarios down to Aigosthena in about 6 h.
vilia.s: in2life.gr; driverstories.gr; zougla.gr; anevenontas.gr; poymittou.gr. Map pin approximate.

kithairon-base.t: Kithairon summit: the abandoned missile base
p: On the summit of Kithairon (1,409 m) stand the concrete ruins and graffiti of an abandoned Air Force station, under mobile-phone masts and beside the chapel of the Prophet Elias. It was one of the four flights of the 350th NIKE guided-missile squadron founded in 1960, with Keratea, Hymettus and Parnitha. One outbuilding was given to the Elefsina mountaineering club in 1990 as the summit refuge.

The Porto Germeno–Kithairon fire of 31 July 2026 burned the mountain; summit webcam footage shows the damage, the refuge still exists, but no report covers the station or the 1960 chapel by the architect Giannakis. Treat everything here as 'check before going'. The land still belongs to the Ministry of Defence.
kithairon-base.s: go-outdoor.gr; mountainsgreece.com; hellasjournal.com; greekreporter.com, iefimerida.gr (2026 fire).

p: Hidden in a karst doline on Pateras, the round tower of Megalo Vathychori stands 12.5 m high and 6.2 m across, an empty shell with four storeys visible inside. Long thought medieval, it is now dated to the third quarter of the 4th century BC. 500 m away on the farm road a square tower 10 m high carries a brown sign, 'Αρχαίος Πύργος'.

They belong to a chain of at least six towers marking the ancient road to Boeotia. The basins around (Vathychori, the big doline of Megalos Kryftis) are closed hollows hidden from both sea and plain; a large solar park now fills the next one.
vathychori.s: kastra.eu; inthemountains.gr; istoriatonmegaron.blogspot.com. Map pin approximate.

p: Aigosthena was the fortified port of ancient Megara on the Alkyonides gulf: an acropolis of 190 × 80 m joined to the sea by two walls. Its south-east tower, about 18 m high and 8.9 m square, was restored with its floors and opened in 2018: climb all three, past arrow slits on three sides, to the top floor's three catapult windows. Beam sockets show where the floors were.
Find-its: the post-Byzantine chapel of Agios Georgios inside the acropolis, an early Christian basilica in the lower town, and the last tower of the north wall standing half in the sea.

The 31 July 2026 fire burned through Porto Germeno; the culture ministry's inspection of 6 August found that, thanks to regular clearing, the fortress and the Byzantine monuments were not badly affected. Best October to May.

At Psatha, 'To Limanaki' and 'Angelos' sit right on the water with ducks swimming in the harbour; beach bars show it is gentrifying. The Alkyonis trail, a 10.4 km loop of 3–4 h between Psatha and Porto Germeno, passes stone huts, dry-stone walls and ruined farmhouses; waymarks are broken in places and there is no water.

High on west Parnitha, in sight of the Acropolis, the walls of Fyli fortress controlled the road from Athens to Boeotia in the 4th century BC. It is unguarded and free. Find-it: the trail down starts right behind the roofed map board on the flat in front of the fort, and the board is pocked with bullet holes from hunters.

Walk down instead of driving: between Fyli and the fortress, by the Thodora, Dipotama and Giannoula streams, an ancient road surface and rock-cut channels that carried the Fyli spring water downstream survive (2–2.5 h downhill). In 403 BC Thrasyboulos seized Fyli to start the march that overthrew the Thirty Tyrants.
fyli-fortress.s: odysseus.culture.gr; topoguide.gr; eposfilis.gr; parnitha.blogspot.com. Map pin approximate.

p: Moni Kleiston, the 'closed' monastery, sits at 600 m on the lip of the Gkoura gorge. Its katholikon is a two-column cross-in-square. Find the carved dates: 1204 in the narthex, 1677 on a fountain, 1742 on a sanctuary window. Sources date the founding to the 11th or 12th century and the church to anywhere from the 13th to the 17th, so ask the nuns to show the narthex inscription.
During the occupation patriots and Jews were smuggled through the monastery to the guerrillas on the mountain. Above it begins the path to the Cave of Pan.

pan-cave-parnitha.t: Cave of Pan above the Gkoura gorge (Lychnospilia)
p: On Mt Tamilthi, high on the east wall of the Gkoura gorge, the Cave of Pan has a main hall of about 70 × 15 m and a second chamber reached through a raised squeeze. Skias excavated it in 1900 and found thousands of little lamps, hence its name Lychnospilia, the 'cave of lamps'. Menander set his comedy 'Dyskolos' here.

The Gkoura is Parnitha's largest ravine, fed by its biggest spring, which once supplied the west branch of Hadrian's aqueduct; an inscription gives its ancient name as Keladon. Its floor is a regular rescue site: walk the rim and cross at Mesonychti, do not follow the bed.
pan-cave-parnitha.s: mixanitouxronou.gr; fysiolatres.gr; parnitha.blogspot.com; topoguide.gr. Map pin approximate.

haf-museum.t: Hellenic Air Force Museum, Dekeleia (Tatoi) air base
p: The Dekeleia (Tatoi) airfield has been flying since 1918 and was an airline hub for TAE in 1935–41. Under the occupation it was a major Luftwaffe base, used for the 1943 Dodecanese operations. The museum, a unit since 1992, fills a big hangar with salvaged WWII aircraft, among them a Blenheim; outside stand a Phantom, an F-104, a Delta Dagger and a C-47.

You enter through the base gate with ID and walk a marked path. The 'oldest Greek airfield in continuous operation' claim rests on one paper. Dekeleia station on the suburban line opened in 1904 as 'Tatoi', with a grand building because it served the royal palace.

bafi-springs.t: Bafi, Skipiza and Mola springs, high Parnitha
p: Around 70 springs rise on Parnitha above 600 m, where limestone lies on schist. From the Bafi refuge a circuit of about 3 h visits Skipiza (about 1,200 m, the highest) and Mola (the largest free-flowing), past the Agios Petros chapel. Since October 2026 Bafi also has the first wheelchair-accessible trail in a Greek national park.

Look up at Karavola: the radome on its concrete bunker is the 2nd Control and Reporting Centre, 'Mambo', on the summit since 1958 and part of NATO's NADGE from 1976. It and the other summits (Ornio, Kaki Rachi) are closed; see them from the trail. The 2007 fire burned two-thirds of Parnitha's fir forest.
bafi-springs.s: topoguide.gr; newsbeast.gr; anixneuseis.gr; athensattica.com. Map pin approximate.

p: At the end of Aiolidos St, near the Solinari spring, the Aloula quarry was set up as an open-air museum of quarrying in the 1990s by N. Golanda and A. Kouzoupi. You can see the kazarma (barracks with two fireplaces), the smithy, the worked faces and the tips of waste marble pouring down the slope. It closed in 1972, so the faces mix pre-war and post-war work.

Dionysos itself was founded by post-war marble cutters from Tinos, Karpathos and Andros and only became a community in 1979. The working Dionysos quarries across the ravine still supply marble for the Acropolis restoration.

In myth Dionysos taught Ikarios to make wine here, and Thespis, the first actor, came from this deme. The fenced site keeps the theatre's proedria seats, a Pythion, a choregic monument and reliefs. Up the Rapentosa stream a shallow hollow scoured by a small waterfall may have been used in the rites. The claim that it is Attica's oldest sanctuary of Dionysos (6th century BC) is a claim.

On the east side of Penteli, 4 km up from the Vraila stop past Pikermi, the old katholikon of Daou Pentelis is a single nave under a hexagonal dome that mixes Byzantine and Islamic elements, described as the only example of its type. Its eight altars point to a 'sleepless' monastery with round-the-clock services. A huge new church stands beside it; one visitor's verdict is 'huge and ugly'.

On Easter night 1680 Algerian pirates killed the monks; saint.gr says only a priest and his disciple, away at a dependency, survived. Their tomb was found under the floor in September 1965 and the Ecumenical Patriarchate canonised them in 1992.
The setting has burned in recent fires; no damage report on the monastery was found.

agios-efraim.t: Agios Efraim monastery, Nea Makri (Kontoglou's grave)
p: On Mt Amomon above Nea Makri, the Evangelismos convent is one of Greece's busiest pilgrimages, for St Efraim, said to have died under torture on a mulberry tree in 1426; the tree is now enclosed in its own small building. Fotis Kontoglou, the painter who led the return to Byzantine icon style, is buried in the courtyard, and his unfinished icon of the saint hangs left of the church door.
agios-efraim.s: el.wikipedia; godbless.gr; parapolitika.gr. Map pin approximate.

vrana-tumuli.t: Vrana: the 'Plataeans' tumulus' and the Bronze Age graves
p: Around the Marathon museum at Vrana are three sites in one walk. About 150 m from the museum inside the fence is the half-excavated 'Tumulus of the Plataeans', with eleven male burials of the early 5th century BC; calling it the grave of Marathon's Plataean dead is contested. Next to the museum a cluster of Middle Bronze Age tumuli (2000–1600 BC), three under a 2004 shelter, includes a pit with a Mycenaean horse burial.

On Plataion St towards the museum, the Early Bronze Age cemetery of Tsepi (3000–2300 BC) has rectangular family tombs with Cycladic links, dug by Marinatos in 1970–73. The museum's Egyptian-style statues come from the Brexiza sanctuary.

oinoi-cave.t: Cave of Pan at Oinoi and the Pythion tower
p: The Cave of Pan at Oinoi was lived in and used for burials in the Late Neolithic (5300–3200 BC), then became a cult cave of Pan and the Nymphs, with Cybele, Artemis and Hermes; a stele of 61/60 BC laid down the rules for visitors. It was excavated in 1958 and again in 2014–18 to stop looting. Find-it: its entrance is sealed with big stones on a small flat just above and right of the open cave Oinoi IV, which many guides wrongly call the Cave of Pan.

Nearby is the Pythion, a sanctuary of Pythian Apollo at a large spring from which Athens' delegation set out for Delphi, and a medieval tower, now fenced. In the 2024 fire the vegetation of the fenced Oinoi site burned and its post-Byzantine Agioi Apostoloi chapel was seriously damaged.
oinoi-cave.s: odysseus.culture.gr; fysiolatres.gr; marathonpress.gr; orthodoxianewsagency.gr (Ephorate inspection, Aug 2024).

p: Beside the chapel of Panagia Mesosporitissa stands a marble rebuild of the trophy set up around 460 BC: a plain shaft and Ionic capital, about 10 m high from twelve drums, in Manolis Korres's 2017 reconstruction. Eugene Vanderpool found the capital and drums built into a medieval tower in 1965; the originals are in the museum.
A trophy (tropaion) was put up where the enemy turned and ran, so one reading is that it marks where the Persian dead fell, not the Athenian line.

brexiza.t: Brexiza: Herodes Atticus's sanctuary of the Egyptian gods
p: Behind the beach at Brexiza, in the marshy edge of Schinias, lies a square precinct with four gates and a stepped central platform: the sanctuary of the Egyptian gods built by Herodes Atticus around 160 AD, with a luxury bath beside it. Plaster copies of Osiris and Isis stand on the gate pylons. It was found in 1968 while a hotel was being built and has been an organised site since 2001; digging continues.

Find-it: in the Marathon museum (gallery 5) the over-life-size Isis wears a cobra headdress and holds three wild roses. Herodes, the richest man of 2nd-century Greece, was from Marathon; Egyptian cults were fashionable with the Roman elite.
brexiza.s: lifo.gr; emena.gr (Siskou, East Attica Ephorate); welovemarathon.gr; travel.gr (2026).

schinias.t: Schinias: Olympic rowing course, the airfield and Makaria spring
p: The 2004 Olympic rowing and canoe course was cut into the Schinias wetland for €88m, over environmental objections, and left abandoned after the Games. The Hellenic Olympic Committee restored it with Alpha Bank money and it reopened on 16 May 2026; it is now the base of the rowing and triathlon federations. Underneath it lay Marathon airfield (1973–2001), where Aegean Airlines started; no relics are known.

At the north-west edge the Makaria spring wells up into two small deep pools; it alone once fed the wetland with 6–7 million m³ of water a year, and it has an endemic minnow, Pelasgus marathonicus. It has been brackish all year since at least the 1990s, a sign of pumping or seawater intrusion. NECCA records more than 240 bird species at Schinias.

kato-souli.t: Kato Souli: Greece's tallest mast, for submarines
p: The Hellenic Navy's Kato Souli transmitter covers 260 ha and has worked since 1989. Its 250 m guyed mast, the tallest structure of its kind in Greece, sends low-frequency signals that reach submarines under water; NTUA engineers strengthened it in 2000–01. With the Nea Makri station it worked as a pair: transmit here, receive there.

A US Navy transmitter stood nearby. In the Souli marshes Y-shaped wooden cable supports, cut steel cables and a generator building are reported, but the only photos come from a fringe blog; verify the objects, ignore the 'time-portal' stories.
kato-souli.s: el.wikipedia; xeneco.gr (Pikros, 2019); attikanea.info. Map pin approximate.

p: The hill above Rafina, 299 stremmata now owned by the municipality, was a German Festung: two anti-aircraft batteries and an observation tower on top, ten or more pillboxes round the slopes, and below them concrete galleries where ammunition moved on rail carts. Guided tours have described an underground shelter about 18 m deep; iRafina measured a 14.5 m ventilation shaft.

The Germans left on 12 October 1944 and blew the fort up, leaving a crater about 12 m deep and 50 m across, but the galleries came through intact. On the shore 14 gun positions and a 500 m stone wall completed the defence. Today a café ('Oxyro') and a playground sit next to the ruins.

agios-nikolaos-rafina.t: Agios Nikolaos, Rafina: a church on a pillbox
p: The little white church of Agios Nikolaos on the hill above Rafina port was built in 1947 on top of a German or Italian pillbox. The pillbox itself, now its basement, became the chapel of Agia Marina, a memorial to the twenty Rafinians arrested by the Germans on 17 July 1944 and saved; only one, Alexandridis, was killed.
More positions lie around it (Panorama, Agia Marina), said to be tunnel-linked to the fortress hill. Rafina's first mole was built in 1907 by Alexandros Skouzes.

asimakis.t: Ta Kavouria tou Asimaki, Rafina port
p: Asimakis Kalpakis started out in the 1950s serving crabs from the bow of a concrete ship moored in Rafina harbour; the present premises date from 1961, the owner's claim backed by a local history. A good place to wait for a ferry.

At Marikes, south of Rafina, a pair of Italian pillboxes, one with '1943' cast in the concrete, are joined by a corridor. Their rails probably came from the Diastavrosi lignite mines' narrow-gauge line. The beach was mined in 1941. Rafina's lignite was mined from 1915 to the 1960s by miners from Kymi; a memory exhibition opened in 2018 by the Rafina Health Centre.

askitario.t: Askitario: a 3000 BC acropolis and German gun pits
p: On Cape Krokodilos, 3 km south of Rafina, the hill of Askitario carries an acropolis founded around 3000 BC (excavated by Theocharis in 1954–55) and a hermit's cave that gave it its name. Over them lie German trenches, gun pits, anti-tank positions, ammunition stores and shelters built with forced labour. There is almost no signage, so read it yourself: Bronze Age walls below, 1940s concrete on top.

Rhamnous sits alone above the strait to Euboea: the sanctuary of Nemesis and Themis on a terrace, a road lined with family grave enclosures, and a fortress over two harbours where Athens kept a garrison to watch the grain ships. The walk from the entrance to the fortress is about a mile on steep dirt.

On 5 August 2026 the culture ministry presented a plan for the south-east fortress walls, the conservation of twelve funerary monuments, signage and fire protection, so parts may be fenced. A small taverna stands by the site.

About 1.5 km north-east of Varnavas a square Classical tower (sides about 6.5 m, standing 3.5 m, door to the south) rises above Agia Paraskevi; about 450 m north-west a Frankish tower 11 m high was partly built from its stones. Dates for the ancient one conflict (5th or 4th century BC).

The Ephorate's report on the August 2024 fire said isolated monuments were 'not damaged' but did not name these towers. In the village, the folklore museum (a 19th-century farmhouse with a wine press) and the bread museum are open weekday mornings (22950 97870).
varnavas-towers.s: varnavasnews.blogspot.com; el.wikipedia; odysseus.culture.gr. Map pin approximate.

p: Kotroni, between Kapandriti and Afidnes, is probably the acropolis of the deme of Aphidna, where Theseus hid Helen after carrying her off, and the home deme of Kallimachos, the polemarch who died at Marathon. The University of Athens has excavated since 2005, exposing the inner circuit wall in 2011–16 and finding obsidian blades. Its slopes burned in August 2024; the excavated remains were untouched.
kotroni.s: el.wikipedia (Afidna); o-pharosva.gr; orthodoxianewsagency.gr (Aug 2024). Map pin approximate.

p: In the Mavrodilesi glen beside a stream, the sanctuary of the hero Amphiaraos worked as a healing oracle in the 5th–4th centuries BC. Patients sacrificed a ram, slept on its skin in the long incubation stoa and waited for a dream; there are baths, a theatre with marble seats of honour, and statue bases along the terraces.
Find-it: cross to the far bank of the stream for the quieter terraces. Visitors note that it is almost always empty.

strofyli-terminus.t: Dionysos station: terminus of the marble railway
p: Two roofless stone buildings on Leoforos Dionysou, about 200 m before the quarry gate, are the terminus of the 9.2 km metre-gauge railway from Kifisia, built by Grecian Marbles ('Marmor' Ltd) and ballasted with marble chips. It carried Pentelic marble from 1899 to 1914, restarted under Bowman in 1922 and closed in 1931. North and west walls stand; a marble sculpture park and the summer 'Dionysia' events use the site.
In the 19th century excursionists rode the line and walked up to picnic at Agios Petros on the Penteli saddle; no cableway or inclined plane from the quarries has been confirmed.
strofyli-terminus.s: odosdionysou.gr (Karafotiou); dionysos.gr; mixanitouxronou.gr; topoguide.gr. Map pin approximate.

thorikos.t: Thorikos: the odd theatre and the mine quarter
p: On the west slope of Velatouri hill the theatre of Thorikos is the strangest in Greece: not a semicircle but an elongated ellipse, built about 525–480 BC and enlarged from about 2,000 to 3,200 seats. Inscriptions south of it record drama performances. Visitors note it was never rebuilt with new stone; half is restored, half left as found.

Thorikos was a mining town. 250 m west of the theatre lies its 'industrial quarter' of houses and ore workshops, beside Gallery No. 3, opened in the late Neolithic, worked to the 4th century BC and again in the 5th–7th centuries AD. Find-it: a plan of the gallery is cut into the marble at its entrance, next to a 4th-century BC inscription. The galleries are closed.

On the hill's saddle and east side are five Mycenaean tombs (1600–1100 BC), three of them tholoi; the big one has lost its roof but keeps its relieving triangle. Reach them on a rough track off the road to the power station.

lavrio-town.t: Lavrio town: the Clock, the miners' monument and the refugee house
p: Modern Lavrio was built from the 1860s by the companies that reopened the ancient mines. Sit at the 'Roloi' (Clock), the gatehouse of the Hellenic Metallurgical Company of about 1870–80, now a café on the port. Opposite is the town hall (1864), the first building of the new town, office and house of the Serpieri–Roux director. The workers' quarters are named after where people came from: Santorineika, Spaniolika.

On the central square a miners' monument honours 'all the foreigners who worked in Lavrio', set against the statue of the Italian industrialist Serpieri (who is buried in Athens, not here). In April 1896 about 1,800 miners struck for two weeks; Wikipedia says four workers and several guards were killed, and the strike won a rise from 2.5 to 3.5 drachmas.

At Dounakara 1 stands the refugee centre that took in political refugees from 1947, later Kurds and Turkish exiles; it was evacuated on 5 July 2023 and its future (car park or hotel) is undecided. The small Mineralogical Museum shows Lavreotiki's famous minerals, more than 600 species, 23 first described here.
lavrio-town.s: lavrioguide.gr; geoparklavreotiki.gr; in.gr; efsyn.gr; el.wikipedia; mdpi.com (Zaimis 2021).

p: South of Lavrio port the shore is built of slag: about 500,000 tonnes of glassy silicate waste from the smelters, with 1–2% lead, 7% zinc and 21–25% iron. Measured lead runs from 5,000 to 51,200 mg/kg, and IGME studies tie children's blood lead in the town to the waste; a beach clean-up was done in 2014.
The ancients left their own slag, poorer in silver than ours could extract; the Italian and French companies of the 1860s came to resmelt it, which is how modern Lavrio began.
lavrio-slag.s: emena.gr (IGME, Dimitriadis et al.); oryktosploutos.net; KPE Lavreotiki. Map pin approximate.

agia-varvara-lavrio.t: Agia Varvara, Lavrio's Catholic company church
p: On the slope above the Technological Park stands the Catholic church of Agia Varvara (St Barbara, patron of miners), a mix of Gothic and neoclassical built for the French company's workers and consecrated on 4 December 1881; the official listing says built 1880, and the often-repeated '1865' is probably wrong. Serpieri's organ came from London in 1881 and was played in a concert around 2025; 'the oldest church organ in Greece' is tour lore.

Below, beside a gallery entrance in the Park, former workers of the mining company set a small icon of St Barbara into the rock; every 4 December a doxology there is followed by loukoumades and cognac. A second Catholic church, the Sacred Heart, stands in the miners' village of Kamariza.

kamariza.t: Kamariza: Serpieri shaft No. 1 and the miners' museum
p: The mining village of Kamariza (renamed Agios Konstantinos in 1954) sits above four interconnected mines of the French company, Serpieri, Christiana, Ilarion and Jean-Baptiste, with about 50 km of galleries below. Serpieri Shaft No. 1 was sunk over an ancient shaft: 165 m deep, five levels, tens of kilometres of railed galleries, with an iron headframe and two lifts.

Find the gatehouse called 'Paron' ('present!'), where miners were counted before going down, and the miner's statue in the village centre. The Mineralogical-Mining Museum in the shaft building was founded by local miners and gives talks on their daily life; the 1896 strike's anniversary is marked here. Mining stopped in 1977, metallurgy in 1981. The site was listed in 1987.

egkoilo-chaos.t: Egkoilo Chaos: a collapsed cave 55 m deep
p: Just past Agios Konstantinos a signed path leads to the Egkoilo Chaos, a collapse sinkhole 55 m deep and about 120 m across, where the roof of a karst cave fell in. Plant fossils are found nearby. Keep well back from the edge: it is not fenced.

In the pine valley of Souriza and Agrileza stand the stone remains of seven ore washeries of the 5th–4th centuries BC: cisterns, settling channels and washing tables where water separated heavy galena from crushed rock, then was collected and reused because water was scarce. This is the silver that paid for the fleet at Salamis.

Two routes with plenty of explanatory signs start at the chapel of Agia Triada Sourizas; an Ephorate archaeologist led the press along them in April 2026. Visitors advise skipping the fenced 'Drymos' entry that needs an appointment and walking the open trail 500 m further.
Sounion National Park (1974) is full of open shafts hidden by vegetation: stay on the path. The whole district is an archaeological zone, so don't collect minerals.
souriza-washeries.s: archaiologia.gr (APE-MPE, Apr 2026); efaanat.gr; civilprotection.gov.gr; Google reviews.

plaka-galleries.t: Plaka: gallery 80 and the Villia inscriptions
p: At Plaka the French company drove gallery '80' in 1954–56 at 80 m altitude as its main haulage gallery, vaulted in stone with ore chutes, and worked it until 1977. It was proposed as a show mine but remains, in the geologists' words, unfinished and not officially or safely open; restoration is on the list of park works.

Nearby the Villia gallery has miners' wall inscriptions dated to the early 20th century. Around Plaka the Adami, Christiana and Ilarion workings carry molybdenum-bearing ore. Watch the Lavreotiki Geopark for guided underground visits.
plaka-galleries.s: oryktosploutos.net (Bitzios, Katsaros); Pemptousia TV (Jun 2025). Map pin approximate.

p: On the hill opposite the temple of Poseidon stands the shell of the 1960s Belvedere hotel. According to the architect Vivi Miliou it closed for good in 1989 and was looted; a University of Thessaly project gives 1960–92 for the 'Belvedere Park'. A new owner fenced it with barbed wire in 2016.

High on the east side of Hymettus above Paiania, the Koutouki cave was found by chance in 1926, mapped in 1954 and opened to visitors in 1960; a guided route of about 350 m runs through its stalactite halls. The road up is about 4 km, the last 2 km rough, with a wide view over the Mesogeia.

Its status has wobbled: odysseus.culture.gr said 'temporarily closed pending takeover by the municipality'; the Ministry told Parliament it opens daily 08:00–15:30. In summer check civilprotection.gov.gr, because on high fire-risk days the road is shut.

Ian Vorres, a Greek-Canadian, came back to Paiania and spent decades filling 18 stremmata with old farmhouses, everyday objects from across Greece and a collection of modern Greek art, set in walled Mediterranean gardens. The museum opened in 1983. Guides show you his own living quarters, a 'Greek time capsule'; there is a good café.

One of the oldest churches of the Mesogeia, built about 1020–30 on top of older remains that you can see in its walls. Inside are two layers of frescoes; the Pantokrator in the dome mixes iconographic types. It is usually locked, so plan for 6 August, or look at the masonry from outside. The Metropolis lists about 110 Byzantine and post-Byzantine chapels in the Mesogeia, most opened only on their feast day.

kontra-chapel.t: Agios Nikolaos on Kontra hill, Koropi
p: Two kilometres south of Koropi, up G. Georga or Zinonos street, a triconch chapel stands alone on the Kontra ridge: three apses in a clover plan, rare in Attica. Its painted templon of the late 17th or early 18th century comes from the school of Georgios Markos, the Athenian painter whose workshop decorated many Mesogeia churches.

kalyvia-churches.t: Kalyvia chapels: Mesosporitissa, Agios Petros, Taxiarches
p: West of Kalyvia, in the area called 'Ennea Pyrgoi', Panagia Mesosporitissa is an 11th–12th-century basilica with a later domed chapel and 18th-century frescoes (the 1902 icons are 'the only false note'); Agios Petros next to it has Byzantine frescoes. In the village the Taxiarches has up to three fresco layers, two Byzantine and one by Georgios Markos, and early Christian sculpture in its templon; it is closed to visitors under the Ephorate except at its big feast.

On a 315 m hill between Keratea and Lavrio stands a ruined fort. Eugene Vanderpool argued that rebel mine slaves built it in the late 2nd century BC, when the Lavrio slaves rose; Lohmann (1995) disputes it. It is under Zone A protection, yet unguarded and looted.
In 2010–11 the state sited a landfill on its edge, and Keratea fought riot police for months in the 'Keratea uprising'. Ancient slaves and modern rubbish on one hill.
ovriokastro.s: archaiologia.gr; el.wikipedia; forkeratea.com. Map pin approximate.

p: Building Athens airport at Spata meant excavating the plain. The collection on the departures level shows 177 objects: two Geometric burials from the cemetery at the north edge (Spata–Loutsa road), finds from a 4th–2nd-century BC pottery workshop at Vathy Pigadi, and a copy of the famous Spata sphinx. During the works a church was moved 340 m west; 11th-century graves round it showed it had been a cemetery church.

perati.t: Perati: a Mycenaean traders' cemetery, Porto Rafti
p: On the south slope of Perati hill, along a ravine north-west of the Erotospilia, a Late Mycenaean community of the 12th century BC cut 192 chamber tombs (some sources say 218). Their Egyptian and Syro-Palestinian amulets, now in the National Archaeological Museum and Brauron, show a port still trading after the palaces fell. The municipality cleared the site in recent years; climb Perati ridge (307 m) for sunrise over the islets.
perati.s: namuseum.gr; mesogianews.gr; efsyn.gr; el.wikipedia. Map pin approximate.

koroni-raftis.t: Koroni fort and the 'Tailor' of Porto Rafti
p: The Koroni peninsula carries a 3rd-century BC fortification above an unorganised beach; the whole peninsula was declared archaeological in 1977, just after holiday-home settlers arrived. From here look out to Raftis islet at the bay entrance, where a headless seated marble figure sits: the 'Raftis' (tailor).

Sources disagree on almost everything about it: male or female, 2nd century BC or Roman, 2.35 m or '4.5 m'. Martoni recorded two statues in 1395; Fauvel is said to have taken the second. The name may really come from an Albanian word for a little plane tree.
koroni-raftis.s: discoverportorafti.gr; el.wikipedia; irafina.gr. Map pin approximate.

p: On Krevati hill above Vari, at 260 m, a cave sacred to the Nymphs, Pan and the Charites holds one of the most personal monuments of Classical Greece. Archedamos of Thera, who called himself 'nympholeptos', seized by the nymphs, tended it in the 5th century BC: he carved a relief of himself with hammer and set-square, a garden, and inscriptions saying he built it all.

The American School excavated it in 1901; its votive reliefs are in the National Archaeological Museum. Byron, King Otto and Queen Amalia visited. In 2020 an illegal party damaged it, and there are no organised visits now; the entrance drops vertically and a hiking guide advises against going down. Go to the mouth, read the carvings in photographs, and imagine the rest.
vari-cave.s: Ephorate of Palaeoanthropology–Speleology; archaiologia.gr (Mari, Archaiologia 144, 2024); notia.gr; en.wikipedia.

p: In the 1960s the tourist board (EOT) built a chain of 'people's beaches'. Varkiza's buildings were designed under Aris Konstantinidis, then head of EOT's design office, the architect of the Xenia hotels. In November 2023 the municipality sublet it for 25 years to Black Wave Varkiza at €1.31m a year plus 6% of turnover; the plan keeps the EOT buildings.

In July 2026 noupou.gr described 'an image of abandonment and decay': the investment of more than €15m had stalled over changes in the investor group, with works now aimed at summer 2027. Come in winter to see the original buildings before they change.

vouliagmeni-lake.t: Lake Vouliagmeni and its flooded cave
p: Lake Vouliagmeni lies under a limestone cliff where an underground cave roof collapsed. Its water, mixing sea and fresh springs, stays warm all year, and small fish nibble your feet. It is now a paid lido.

Behind it a flooded cave has been mapped to 3,123 m. At 105 m depth, 730 m in, divers found a giant stalagmite: stalagmites cannot grow under water, so the cave was dry when the sea stood far lower in the Ice Age. Eight divers have died in it; a ministry decision closed it to the public in 1995.
Offshore at the second Limanaki the 'Devil's Well', a shaft at 11 m depth explored to about 150 m and thought to link to the lake, has killed divers since 1978; grilles now bar it.

Astir Vouliagmeni on the Laimos peninsula is the showpiece of 1960s Greek resort modernism: master plan of 1958 by Vourekas, Sakellarios, Vasileiadis and Dekavallas, beach opened in August 1960, the first 76 'kampanes' (bell) bungalows by Voutsinas in 1961, the Arion hotel by Vourekas and Georgiadis in 1967. It is now a privatised luxury resort, so see it from the road. The Vouliagmeni Nautical Club by Antonis Kitsikis (1959) was the first building in the area.
astir-vouliagmeni.s: athensvoice.gr; protothema.gr; iciao.gr. Map pin approximate.

p: At about km 36 of the Athens–Sounio road, in Agia Marina of Koropi, stand the concrete frames of the ILIOS hotel, begun in the 1970s for more than 400 rooms on 65 stremmata, with bungalows and a tunnel to the beach. Never finished, it was looted and graffitied, and once belonged to the banker Koskotas.

HIG bought it in 2023 and its Ella Resorts plan 339 rooms with a bridge and underpass to the beach; the environmental study for completing the buildings was in public consultation in January–March 2026. The existing frames are to be finished and renovated, not demolished, so the ruin is ending.
althea-hotel.s: ered.gr (20 Jan 2026); mesogianews.gr; euro2day.gr; reader.gr. Map pin approximate.

p: Salt appears on maps of Anavyssos from 1520. Refugees from Phocaea in Asia Minor worked the pans from 1924; they closed in 1969 and were declared a tourist public estate. Rubble dumping is degrading them. The Kalyvia library's digital archive has 1936 photos of salt workers on the narrow-gauge salt rails, good for a then-and-now.

On a cliff over the sea at Kakia Thalassa on the Keratea coast stands the shell of the Manoleio–Spyrideio foundation, a charitable home linked to an abbess Mariam whose second phase was left unfinished after 2004. Graffiti earned it the name 'psychedelic building'; it has been used to dump stolen cars and collects ghost stories. It is unstable: look from outside.
kakia-thalassa.s: urbex.gr; mikropragmata.lifo.gr; mixanitouxronou.gr. Map pin approximate.

p: Finished in 2003 for the 2004 Games, the equestrian centre and racetrack at 'Pousi Bartzi – Merenta' covers 996,920 m². Racing stopped in 2024 and the equine clinic shut. Auctions failed; the Hellenic Growth Fund then received three bids for a 99-year surface right, from the Equestrian Federation, a Melissanidis company and Mytilineos's Elia. Next to it the Olympic shooting centre is now a live-firing police range.
markopoulo-equestrian.s: powergame.gr; capital.gr; ypodomes.com; oneman.gr. Map pin approximate.

routes.name: Acropolis, the hills and the Observatory
routes.when: Start at the Acropolis opening slot; the Observatory visitor centre opens in the evening, so end there or come back.
routes.summary: The Acropolis for its curves and scars, the quiet North Slope caves, the Theatre of Dionysus, then over the Areopagus to Pikionis's paths, the Pnyx and the Observatory hill.

routes.name: Agora, Monastiraki and Psyrri
routes.when: Agora from 8:00; Kerameikos reopened Sept 2026.
routes.summary: From the boundary stone of the Agora through Hadrian's Library and the Eridanos in the metro to the Tower of the Winds, the Medrese gate, the churches built of other buildings, the column chapel and the Kerameikos gate.

routes.name: Syntagma and Panepistimiou: Occupation and ideas
routes.when: Do Korai 4 in the morning (Tue–Sat 9–14); Old Chemistry library Mon–Fri.
routes.summary: The Unknown Soldier and the metro strata, the Gestapo house and the Kommandantur cells, Zonar's, Parnassos and Koun's basement theatre, the old National Library and the Catholic cathedral, ending at the Old Chemistry lab.

routes.name: Market and Omonia
routes.when: Lunchtime for Diporto; the bank opens on weekdays.
routes.summary: Down Athinas and Aiolou: the Themistoclean gate inside a bank, the car park that became a dig, a sign-less basement tavern, Kaftanzoglou's Omonia church and the vanished railway square.

routes.name: Plaka, the Olympieion and the buried river
routes.when: Cemetery 7:30–20; Saita and Brettos in the evening.
routes.summary: From Zenetos's sliding façade by the Garden through the Russian and Anglican churches to Hadrian's temple and arch, the open Ilisos, the stadium tunnel, the Ardittos shelter hill and the First Cemetery.

routes.name: Kolonaki and Lycabettus
routes.when: Climb to Agioi Isidoroi before noon; the theatre only on concert nights.
routes.summary: Modernist blocks round the National Garden's edge, the Conservatory and the Lyceum, the column of Kolonaki and Papadiamantis's square, Pikionis's school and the German church, then up to the cave church, its shelter and Zenetos's theatre.

routes.name: Exarchia, Alexandras and Kypseli
routes.when: Polytechnic closed around 17 November.
routes.summary: The Polytechnic gate, the Blue Building and the Exarchia cinemas, Atelier 66's street stair, the junta's Bouboulinas site, the Averof stele and the Prosfygika, then Kypseli's 1930s street and a shelter with its steel doors.

routes.name: Ambelokipi and Goudi: towers, the junta and science
routes.when: Criminology Museum by appointment only; Mineralogy Museum Mon–Fri 9:30–14.
routes.summary: The glass towers of the 1970s, the junta's last Security HQ, Valsamakis's first block, the Pasteur Institute, the last guillotine, the Olympic badminton hall and the brutalist student slab of Zografou.

routes.name: West Athens: Finos to Votanikos
routes.when: Campus hours for Hasekis's konaki.
routes.summary: Finos Film's building, the Peloponnese station, Plato's Academy, the only Ottoman fountain, the city's first mosque and the train turned theatre.

routes.name: Piraeus: ships, shelters and the Blockade
routes.when: Mantra mornings Tue–Fri; Lipasmata park open late.
routes.summary: Trireme sheds through a basement window, the Kastella shelters and the 1960s cave club, the old kafeneia and German batteries, the ghost factories, the fertiliser park and the dragon power station, then Nikaia's Blockade wall and cemetery.

routes.name: The south shore: power, Olympics and refugees
routes.when: EMST closed Monday; Phaleron cemetery daytime.
routes.summary: FIX's façades and Dourgouti's refugee blocks, Nea Smyrni's December 1944, the 1903 power station and the beach-volleyball white elephant, the sea-facing war cemetery, Zenetos's round school and the Panagoulis station, down to the old airport and Glyfada's modern churches.

routes.name: Kaisariani and Hymettus
routes.when: Shooting Range enclosure opens irregularly.
routes.summary: The wall of the 200, the refugee blocks of 'Little Moscow', the monastery spring and the German station ruins near the summit.

routes.name: Penteli and the north (car)
routes.when: Car needed. End at the Newall telescope for an evening show.
routes.summary: Workers' housing and a cave in the suburbs, the one-day church of Galatsi, the junta broadcasting house and the reactor, the sanatorium shells, the NATO dishes, the Parthenon's quarry cave, the German cemetery and the marble telescope.

routes.name: Mesogeia, Lavrio and Sounion (car)
routes.when: Car needed; a full day. Sounion at sunset.
routes.summary: Brauron's bridge and pillboxes at Porto Rafti, the NIKE missile base, Lavrio's ore washeries and railway, then Sounion for Byron's name.

routes.name: Halandri: the stream, the station and a Roman tomb
routes.when: On foot or by bike. Library and Aetopouleio on weekdays; Rematia best in the morning or for a summer show.
routes.summary: The old Lavrio-line station and its buried rails, the village square, a Roman mausoleum used as a church, the lost distillery and a crumbling villa, then up the protected stream to the Frankish chapel site.

routes.name: Cholargos and Papagou: the Six, the Pentagon and the nuns
routes.when: By bike; end at the Theologos convent in its morning hours, then up the Hymettus track.
routes.summary: The banknote works and the 'Pentagon' on Mesogeion, the grove where the Six were shot in 1922, the Italian HQ villa, the officers' garden suburb and a Hymettus convent whose date nobody agrees on.

routes.name: Agia Paraskevi: the square, the reactor and Kynigos
routes.when: By bike; the climb to Kynigos is steep. Kynigos opens 7–10 and 16–19.
routes.summary: A listed summer cinema on the old square, a painter's studio kept as he left it, Greece's only nuclear reactor behind its fence, and the hilltop monastery of the 'Hunter'.

routes.name: Psychiko: the company plan, the sculptor and Orlandos
routes.when: On foot from Faros; the Zongolopoulos house opens on weekdays.
routes.summary: A garden suburb drawn by a company in 1923: round squares, a Catholic institute, Orlandos's church with a mysterious icon stand, the royal villa, a sculptor's studio, two interwar schools, and the refugee square of Neo Psychiko.

routes.name: Tourkovounia and Filothei: quarries, a 1944 grave and the crypt
routes.when: On foot or mountain bike; the quarry basin has sharp drops. Karamanlis Foundation weekdays.
routes.summary: The quarries that built Psychiko, the broken crosses of 1944, Zeus's peak altar, the Karamanlis grave, the bank clerks' garden city, the cave crypt of St Filothei, the lost Rotonda, the last Lavrio-line rails and a ceramicist's 1965 house.

routes.name: Elefsina's factory seafront (suburban rail)
routes.when: Proastiakos to Elefsina. Most factories are exterior only; IRIS and the Oil Mill open on event days.
routes.summary: Soap, spirits, paint and cement along 2.5 km of shore: the 1875 soap works by the sanctuary, the Mysteries, the IRIS chimney, the concrete Kronos distillery, Titan's lost Cave of Pan and the 1941 airfield.

routes.name: Megara, Vourkari and Kakia Skala
routes.when: Proastiakos to Megara, then a car or taxi for Kakia Skala and Ierotheos. Phone the Megara museum about the fountain.
routes.summary: A 1950 mill, flamingos and an 1821 wall, the old station, the biggest ancient fountain in Greece, German posts on the cliff railway of Skiron, and a monastery that hid British soldiers.

routes.name: The frontier: Kaza pass to Aigosthena (car)
routes.when: Car needed; a full day. Check the Kithairon summit after the July 2026 fire. October to May.
routes.summary: Along the old border of Athens, Thebes and Megara: a Byzantine monastery, a lone tower, the twelve-towered Gyftokastro, a mountain village, the NIKE ruins on Kithairon, the climbable tower of Aigosthena, a harbour lunch and the Vathychori towers on the way back.

routes.name: West Parnitha: Fyli, Kleiston and Pan's cave
routes.when: Car or bus to Fyli; hiking boots and a torch. October to May; hunting in season.
routes.summary: A 4th-century BC fort reached on an ancient road, a monastery on the lip of a gorge, and the cult cave where Menander set his play.

routes.name: Tatoi and high Parnitha (car)
routes.when: Car needed. The museum is inside an active base: bring ID.
routes.summary: WWII aircraft at Dekeleia, the royal estate, the highest springs under the summit radar, and the mountain's casino, sanatorium and burned antenna post.

routes.name: Dionysos: the marble railway and the god's deme
routes.when: Car or bus 536. Book Ikarion with the Ephorate; German cemetery free in the mornings.
routes.summary: The roofless terminus of the 1899 marble railway, a quarry kept as a museum, the deme where wine and drama were born, and the German war cemetery's crypts.

routes.name: Marathon plain and Schinias
routes.when: Car, or KTEL Marathon and walks. Morning for the museum.
routes.summary: The Athenians' mound, Bronze Age graves and the contested Plataeans' tumulus, the sealed Cave of Pan, the dam, the rebuilt trophy, the Olympic course on the old airfield, the submarine mast, and Herodes's Egyptian sanctuary.

routes.name: Rafina's war coast
routes.when: KTEL Rafina and on foot; Daou needs a car or a 4 km walk from Vraila.
routes.summary: A German fortress hill with galleries and a crater, a church built on a pillbox, a taverna born on a concrete ship, Italian pillboxes dated 1943, a Bronze Age acropolis under German gun pits, and Daou's hexagonal dome.

routes.name: Rhamnous to Oropos (car)
routes.when: Car needed; Rhamnous takes 2 h on steep paths.
routes.summary: Helen's hill at Aphidna, the Varnavas towers, the fortress and Nemesis at Rhamnous, and the healing oracle of the Amphiareion.

routes.name: Lavrio and Thorikos (KTEL)
routes.when: KTEL Athens–Lavrio. Sunday morning to see inside Agia Varvara.
routes.summary: A company town: the Clock café and the miners' monument, lead-laden slag beaches, the French works at Kyprianos with St Barbara's church, Thorikos's elliptical theatre and mine gallery, and the metre-gauge railway.

routes.name: Kamariza and the Sounion forest (car)
routes.when: Car needed. Park closes on high fire-risk days. Stay on the paths: open shafts.
routes.summary: The Serpieri shaft and the miners' museum, a 55 m sinkhole, Plaka's galleries, the ancient ore washeries on signed trails, an abandoned 1960s hotel, then Poseidon.

routes.name: Mesogeia: a cave, chapels and a slaves' fort (car)
routes.days: Vorres weekends; churches on feast days
routes.when: Car needed; weekends for Vorres. Koutouki closes on fire-risk days.
routes.summary: A show cave on Hymettus, an emigrant's folk museum, 11th-century Koropi, a three-apsed hill chapel, the Kalyvia frescoes, a fort perhaps built by rebel mine slaves, and the NIKE base.

routes.name: Porto Rafti and Brauron
routes.when: Car, or KTEL Porto Rafti; the airport collection by metro on the way out or back.
routes.summary: Finds from the airport digs, the dead Olympic racetrack, Artemis's sanctuary, a Mycenaean traders' cemetery, wartime pillboxes and the headless Tailor in the bay.

routes.name: The south coast: Vari to Kakia Thalassa (car)
routes.when: Car needed; winter is best for the architecture.
routes.summary: The nymph-seized stonecutter's cave, Konstantinidis's EOT beach, a lake over a flooded cave, the 1960s Astir, Panagoulis's bomb culvert, the junta's unfinished hotel, salt pans and a psychedelic ruin on a cliff.

tours.name: Church hunt through the ages: one day in the centre
tours.intro: Athens's religious buildings are best where one era sits inside another: a column through a roof, a church made of carvings, a chapel under a ministry, a cave church, a Bauhaus pulpit, a mosque with no minaret. One clue per stop.
tours.how: On foot plus one metro hop to Votanikos (or end at Loumbardiaris). Churches open mornings; the Christuskirche only on Sunday, Agioi Isidoroi 9–12.
story: Athens was a small town when it became the capital in 1834, and the planners of King Otto demolished dozens of Byzantine churches to lay out the new streets; the survivors are scattered among shops and offices. That is why the hunt is good here: every old church is a survivor of a plan.
The order is chronological: early Christian foundations, Byzantine churches built of spolia, Ottoman-era chapels, the Bavarian 19th century, then the modernists and the new mosque.

stops.note: 5th century: trace four apses in the courtyard of Hadrian's Library.
Roman column through a chapel roof; fevers were tied to it with thread. Find the capital among the branches.
12th century (disputed): a church made of about 90 older carvings. Find the calendar frieze of months and zodiac.
11th century, saved by Ludwig I. Find the Roman capitals in the west wall.
11th century, Russian since 1847. Ask about the cistern 5 m under the floor.
Ottoman-era chapel under a 1950s ministry on stilts. Look up: the building is its sky.
1853–65, Klenze. Count the green Tinos columns cut for a palace.
1931–34, Neue Sachlichkeit: Bauhaus-era pulpit and candlesticks (Sunday).
15th–16th century in Lycabettus's biggest cave; read the tunnel plaque.
1954–58, Pikionis: a chapel re-clad in the debris of demolished Athens. Find the neoclassical marble scraps.
2020: the state-built mosque without a minaret. Find the mihrab.

tours.name: Occupied Athens, 1941–44
tours.intro: The Occupation left exact marks: cells with prisoners' graffiti, an execution wall, a factory yard with ricochet scars, a synagogue where a community was rounded up.
tours.how: Two half-days: the centre on foot (Korai 4 Tue–Sat 9–14), then Kaisariani by bus and Nikaia by metro (Mantra Tue–Fri 9–13).
story: Germany, Italy and Bulgaria occupied Greece from April 1941. In Athens the famine of the first winter killed tens of thousands; the resistance (EAM-ELAS) grew strong in the refugee suburbs, and the occupiers answered with reprisals and with 'blockades' of whole districts, where hooded informers picked out men to be shot.

In 1943–44 Haidari camp fed the execution grounds. The Jews of Athens were arrested at their synagogue on 24 March 1944. The Germans left on 12 October 1944; the Dekemvriana fighting between ELAS and the British-backed government followed within weeks.

stops.note: Seat of the German military administration.
SS and Gestapo interrogation centre; the cell door survives.
Kommandantur cells: prisoners' graffiti 6 m underground.
Two waiters arrived in Nazi uniform in 1941, fifth-column spies.
24 March 1944: the round-up of the Jews of Athens.
1 May 1944: 200 shot; they went singing.
The condemned block of the camp.
17 August 1944: the Blockade's execution yard.
Where the Blockade dead lie.
October 1944: ELAS saves the power station from demolition.

tours.name: The junta: torture rooms, a bomb and a gate
tours.intro: The colonels ruled from 21 April 1967 to July 1974. Their places of torture and the places of resistance are small, scattered and mostly unmarked.
tours.how: Centre on foot, then metro to Ambelokipi; Loumbarda and the Panagoulis station by car or tram.
story: On 21 April 1967 a group of colonels took power with tanks from Goudi. Opponents were jailed, tortured and exiled to islands. The Security Police ran Bouboulinas 18 and then Mesogeion 14–18; the Military Police ran EAT-ESA.

Alexandros Panagoulis tried to kill the dictator Papadopoulos in August 1968; the Polytechnic rose in November 1973; the regime fell in July 1974 after the Cyprus disaster. Panagoulis died in a car crash in 1976 that many still think was not an accident.

stops.note: Security HQ to 1971: the rooftop falanga room. Demolished.
Averof prison, demolished 1972.
17 November 1973: the gate a tank crushed.
Where the November 1973 mobilisations began.
The Military Police torture rooms, where Panagoulis was held.
Security HQ 1971–74: two cells survive.
The junta's broadcasting house (begun 1968).
A tower allowed by the junta's relaxed height law.
13 August 1968: Panagoulis's bomb under the coast road.
1 May 1976: where he died.

tours.name: The water of Athens: buried rivers and a marble dam
tours.intro: Athens has always been short of water. Follow it from the tyrants' aqueduct and the buried Eridanos and Ilisos to an Ottoman fountain and the marble-faced dam of 1929.
tours.how: Centre on foot and metro; Marathon dam by car.
story: The ancient city drank from springs and wells, aqueducts built by the Peisistratids and by Hadrian, and the rivers Eridanos and Ilisos. Both rivers now run under the streets: the Eridanos in a Roman channel, the Ilisos under an avenue since the 1930s.
Hadrian's aqueduct served Athens into the 20th century. Only the American Ulen company's Marathon dam (1929) and its tunnel ended the shortages.

tours.name: Science in Athens: telescopes, labs and a reactor
tours.intro: For a chemist: Ziller's laboratory with its hidden radio, an observatory Gagarin visited, a marble-housed telescope, the Pasteur Institute, minerals and a reactor.
tours.how: Old Chemistry on a weekday; observatories in the evening (book); Penteli and Agia Paraskevi by car.
story: Science came to Athens with the Bavarian state: the Observatory (1842) and the university laboratories. Chemistry got its own building in 1887–90, in the age of Hofmann and Christomanos; physics, medicine and bacteriology followed.
After the war the Demokritos centre and its reactor (1961) were Greece's step into nuclear research.

tours.name: Mountains of Attica: sanatoria and Cold War ruins
tours.intro: The hills round Athens hold two layers of ruins: the 1930s sanatoria of the 'Greek Davos' and the radar, radio and missile sites of the Cold War.
tours.how: Car needed; two days (Penteli and Parnitha; Keratea with Lavrio). Stay outside fences.
story: Penteli's and Parnitha's dry air drew tuberculosis sanatoria between the wars. After antibiotics they became hospitals, hotels and schools, and then ruins.

In the Cold War the same hills carried NATO: NIKE missile flights at Keratea, Hymettus, Parnitha and Kithairon from 1960, with US custody of the nuclear warheads; telecom stations on Penteli; a US Navy station at Nea Makri. Most closed by 1990–2005.

tours.name: Modern Athens: Pikionis, Zenetos, Konstantinidis
tours.intro: The best Greek modernists in their own city: Pikionis's turn from modernism to landscape, Zenetos's machines, Konstantinidis's frames, and the interwar blocks that came first.
tours.how: Centre on foot; Nea Filadelfeia and Agios Dimitrios by metro.
story: Athens built one of Europe's best sets of 1930s modernist apartment blocks, in Kypseli, Exarchia and Kolonaki. After the war the polykatoikia became the city's mass housing; a few architects used it to experiment.

Pikionis abandoned his modernist school for the Philopappou paths; Zenetos designed for a future of electronic cities; Konstantinidis built bare frames with earth-coloured infill. Several of their works are already gone.

story: Classical Athens is mostly ruins in a modern city, so the pleasure is in the details: a stone that speaks, a curve in a step, a river still running.

tours.name: Forts of the Attic frontier
tours.intro: Attica was a small state with long borders. Walk the chain of forts and watchtowers that watched its passes and coasts, from Fyli to Rhamnous.
tours.how: Car needed; spread over several day-outs.
story: In the 4th century BC Athens ringed its territory with forts on the passes to Boeotia and the Megarid (Fyli, Eleutherae, Aigosthena on the Megarian side) and with garrison towns on the coast such as Rhamnous. Between them, single towers watched roads and farms.

Who built which fort is still argued: Eleutherae may be Athenian or Theban, the Vathychori towers were once thought medieval, and Ovriokastro may be the work of rebel slaves. Each stop has its own puzzle.

tours.name: Silver of Lavrio: from slaves to the French company
tours.intro: The silver that built Athens's fleet came from the Lavreotiki. Follow it from Neolithic galleries to ancient washeries, the 19th-century companies and the toxic slag they left.
tours.how: Car or KTEL Lavrio; one long day or two.
story: The ancients mined galena (lead sulphide) for its silver, washed the ore with recycled rainwater and smelted it, using thousands of slaves. The Laurion strike of 483 BC paid for the ships that won at Salamis.

From the 1860s Italian and French companies came back to resmelt the ancient slag and then reopen the mines; they built a company town of many nationalities, a Catholic church and a railway. Mining ended in 1977 and metallurgy in 1981, leaving galleries, shafts and slag.
